architecture.description: An AI host uses an MCP client to discover server capabilities, then invokes narrowly scoped tools or reads resources through a negotiated transport.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A small stdio server registers attributed tools from the assembly so compatible clients can discover and call the order-status capability.

bestPractices: Expose small, intention-revealing tools with strict schemas instead of giving a model generic database, shell, or network access.
Authenticate clients, authorize every capability and target resource, and require confirmation for destructive or financially meaningful actions.
Validate inputs and outputs, apply cancellation and timeouts, and return structured errors that do not reveal secrets or internal topology.
Log capability identity, caller, result, latency, and correlation data while redacting prompts, credentials, and sensitive payloads.

interviewQuestions.question: How is MCP different from function calling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Function calling is usually a model-provider feature for requesting a named function. MCP standardizes discovery, schemas, invocation, resources, prompts, transports, and lifecycle between AI hosts and external capability servers.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an MCP server use stdio instead of HTTP?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stdio is a good fit when the host starts and owns a local child process. HTTP is appropriate for independently deployed or remotely shared servers that need network authentication, scaling, and operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main security risk of MCP tools?
interviewQuestions.answer: A model can turn untrusted instructions into real side effects. Tools must enforce the same authentication, authorization, validation, least privilege, and confirmation rules as any other application endpoint.

note: MCP standardizes integration mechanics; it does not decide whether a tool call is safe, permitted, or correct for a particular user.
tip: Start with one read-only tool and test discovery, schema clarity, cancellations, and audit logs before exposing write operations.
warning: Never expose an unrestricted shell, SQL executor, or broad cloud credential as an MCP tool.
latestNote: New guide on MCP servers, clients, tools, resources, and security

name: API Security & OWASP
shortDescription: Design and test ASP.NET Core APIs against common authorization, resource-consumption, configuration, and integration risks.
overview: API security applies identity, authorization, input boundaries, abuse controls, secure configuration, and continuous verification to every exposed operation and object.
detail: The OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights recurring risks including broken object-level authorization, broken authentication, unrestricted resource consumption, sensitive business-flow abuse, server-side request forgery, security misconfiguration, poor API inventory, and unsafe consumption of upstream APIs. ASP.NET Core supplies useful controls, but secure design begins with explicit assets, actors, trust boundaries, deny-by-default policy, and negative tests.

concepts.title: Object-level authorization
concepts.description: Every request for a specific record must verify the caller can access that object; a valid token alone does not prevent identifier-based data exposure.

concepts.title: Abuse and resource controls
concepts.description: Rate limits, request-size limits, pagination, timeouts, quotas, and workflow-specific rules protect compute and sensitive business flows.

concepts.title: Input and output boundaries
concepts.description: Purpose-built request and response models, validation, allowlists, and minimal serialization reduce mass assignment and excessive data exposure.

concepts.title: Inventory and dependencies
concepts.description: Teams must know which API versions and hosts exist, patch them, retire stale endpoints, and treat upstream API responses as untrusted input.

architecture.description: Traffic passes through edge protections and ASP.NET Core security controls before resource-aware authorization permits application logic to access protected data and dependencies.

code.label: OrderEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: The endpoint requires authentication and rate limiting, loads the target resource, then performs resource-aware authorization before returning a minimal response.

bestPractices: Threat-model APIs by asset, actor, trust boundary, and abuse case, then turn the findings into authorization and negative-test requirements.
Authorize the requested resource and tenant on the server for every operation; never trust a client-supplied owner, role, price, or workflow state.
Bound request size, query complexity, page size, concurrency, duration, and outbound destinations instead of relying on one global rate limit.
Maintain an API inventory, remove obsolete versions, patch dependencies, scan configuration, and test security controls in the deployed environment.

interviewQuestions.question: What is broken object-level authorization (BOLA)?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when an API accepts an object identifier but does not verify that the authenticated caller is allowed to act on that specific object, allowing access by changing identifiers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is rate limiting not a complete authorization control?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rate limiting controls volume, not permission. A caller below the limit can still access the wrong tenant, object, function, or business workflow unless authorization is enforced separately.

interviewQuestions.question: How should an API consume an upstream API safely?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authenticate the dependency, restrict destinations, set timeouts and size limits, validate responses, avoid blindly following redirects, and treat returned data as untrusted.

note: The OWASP list is an awareness and prioritization aid, not a substitute for a system-specific threat model.
tip: For every happy-path integration test, add anonymous, wrong-tenant, wrong-owner, oversized-input, and repeated-request cases.
warning: A globally authenticated API can still be critically vulnerable when object and function authorization are missing.
latestNote: New guide aligned with the OWASP API Security Top 10

name: Azure Key Vault & Secrets
shortDescription: Protect application secrets, keys, and certificates with managed identity, Azure RBAC, rotation, and auditable access.
overview: Azure Key Vault centralizes secrets, cryptographic keys, and certificates while Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC control who or what can use them.
detail: A .NET application can load Key Vault secrets through the ASP.NET Core configuration provider or use Azure SDK clients for explicit operations. DefaultAzureCredential supports developer identity locally and managed identity in Azure, avoiding deployed client secrets. Production design must also cover least-privilege data-plane roles, network access, rotation, caching, version behavior, diagnostics, recovery, and separation between environments.

concepts.title: Vault object types
concepts.description: Secrets hold sensitive values, keys support cryptographic operations, and certificates manage certificate material and lifecycle.

concepts.title: Managed identity
concepts.description: An Azure-hosted workload obtains short-lived Entra tokens without storing a client secret in source code or application configuration.

concepts.title: Azure RBAC
concepts.description: Separate control-plane and data-plane roles grant narrowly scoped management or object access and can be audited centrally.

concepts.title: Versions and rotation
concepts.description: Updating a secret creates a version; applications need an intentional refresh, rollout, fallback, and rollback strategy.

architecture.description: The .NET workload uses its Entra identity to request narrowly authorized Key Vault data, while diagnostics and rotation processes govern access throughout the secret lifecycle.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The application adds Key Vault as a configuration source and uses the same credential chain for local development and managed identity in Azure.

bestPractices: Use managed identity for Azure workloads and developer identity or approved local secret storage during development; never commit credentials.
Prefer Azure RBAC data-plane roles, least privilege, separate vaults or strong boundaries per environment, and just-in-time administration.
Design secret rotation with overlapping validity, refresh behavior, observability, rollback, and dependency coordination before an emergency.
Enable diagnostics and alerts, protect recovery settings, restrict network access where appropriate, and avoid logging resolved secret values.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use managed identity with Key Vault?
interviewQuestions.answer: It removes the need to distribute and rotate an application credential for accessing the vault; Azure issues short-lived tokens to the workload identity.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the Key Vault control plane and data plane?
interviewQuestions.answer: The control plane manages the vault resource and settings, while the data plane operates on secrets, keys, and certificates. Permissions should be scoped separately.

interviewQuestions.question: Does rotating a Key Vault secret automatically update every running application?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. A new version becomes available, but each integration has its own caching and refresh behavior. Applications need a tested strategy for observing and adopting the new value.

note: Key Vault protects stored secret material, but callers can still leak a retrieved value through logs, exceptions, telemetry, or overly broad process access.
tip: Test rotation in a non-production environment using two valid credential versions before relying on the process during an incident.
warning: Do not replace one embedded application secret with another embedded credential used to access the vault.
latestNote: New guide on managed identity, RBAC, and secret rotation

name: Internal Developer Platforms
shortDescription: Create product-minded golden paths that give development teams secure, governed, observable self-service delivery.
overview: An internal developer platform (IDP) combines self-service workflows, reusable platform capabilities, and governance to reduce developer cognitive load from idea to production.
detail: Platform engineering treats developers as customers and the platform as a product. An IDP connects templates, source control, CI/CD, infrastructure, secrets, policy, observability, documentation, and service ownership into supported golden paths. For .NET teams, Aspire can standardize local orchestration, service discovery, health checks, telemetry, and deployment models, but it is one building block rather than the entire platform.

concepts.title: Golden paths
concepts.description: Recommended, supported routes encode proven defaults for common workloads while allowing documented escape hatches for genuine exceptions.

concepts.title: Self-service interfaces
concepts.description: Portals, CLIs, APIs, templates, and automation let teams provision and operate services without ticket-driven handoffs.

concepts.title: Platform as a product
concepts.description: A platform team researches developer needs, owns a roadmap and support model, and measures adoption and outcomes rather than mandating tools.

concepts.title: Governance by design
concepts.description: Security, cost, reliability, ownership, and compliance controls are built into reusable workflows with early feedback.

architecture.description: Developers use a portal, CLI, or template to invoke platform APIs that coordinate engineering systems and provision governed runtime capabilities with feedback and telemetry.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: A reusable Aspire composition can form part of a .NET golden path by wiring dependencies, health, service discovery, and local orchestration consistently.

bestPractices: Start with a thin, high-friction developer journey and build the smallest viable golden path with teams that will use it.
Provide APIs, automation, documentation, support, and escape hatches; a catalog page alone is not a developer platform.
Encode secure defaults and policy feedback early, while keeping ownership boundaries and failure recovery visible to product teams.
Measure lead time, onboarding time, reliability, adoption, support load, and developer satisfaction instead of output such as template count.

interviewQuestions.question: How is an internal developer platform different from a developer portal?
interviewQuestions.answer: A portal is one possible user interface. An IDP includes the underlying APIs, automation, templates, policies, infrastructure capabilities, ownership model, and operational feedback.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a golden path?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a supported route for a common workload that packages good defaults and automation to reduce cognitive load without forbidding justified alternatives.

interviewQuestions.question: Where does .NET Aspire fit in platform engineering?
interviewQuestions.answer: Aspire can standardize application composition, local dependencies, service discovery, health, telemetry, and deployment representations for .NET workloads, but CI/CD, cloud provisioning, policy, identity, catalogs, and product ownership still require a broader platform.

note: Successful platforms earn adoption by removing friction; they do not merely centralize control or rename an operations ticket queue.
tip: Interview developers and map one delivery journey before selecting portal or infrastructure products.
warning: A mandatory big-bang platform built without product-team feedback can increase cognitive load and create a new bottleneck.
latestNote: New guide on golden paths, self-service, governance, and Aspire

name: Dapper
shortDescription: Map parameterized SQL to .NET objects with a small, fast API built on standard ADO.NET connections.
overview: Dapper is a lightweight object mapper that extends ADO.NET database connections with APIs for executing parameterized SQL and mapping result rows to .NET types.
detail: Dapper deliberately leaves SQL, connections, transactions, schema evolution, and aggregate persistence decisions to the application. Query, Execute, QuerySingle, multi-mapping, multiple result sets, stored procedures, and asynchronous APIs cover common data-access needs with little abstraction. It is especially useful for explicit read models and performance-sensitive queries, and can coexist with EF Core when boundaries and transaction ownership are clear.

concepts.title: Explicit SQL
concepts.description: The application owns query text, joins, projections, indexes, and provider behavior rather than relying on a LINQ translator.

concepts.title: Parameter binding
concepts.description: Anonymous objects, POCOs, dictionaries, and DynamicParameters bind values safely and support input, output, and return parameters.

concepts.title: Row mapping
concepts.description: Column names map to typed objects, while multi-mapping and QueryMultiple handle joined objects and multiple result grids.

concepts.title: Transaction ownership
concepts.description: Dapper uses the supplied DbConnection and DbTransaction, so application code controls lifetime, atomicity, and coordination.

architecture.description: A query service owns explicit SQL and parameters, Dapper executes through an ADO.NET connection, and projected rows become focused read models.

code.label: OrderQueries.cs
code.introduction: A query object sends parameterized SQL through a provider connection and maps only the columns needed by the read model.

bestPractices: Always bind changing values as parameters; never concatenate user input, sort expressions, identifiers, or filter fragments into SQL.
Project only required columns, bound result sizes, inspect query plans, and add indexes based on measured production-shaped queries.
Open connections late, dispose them predictably, pass explicit transactions when operations must be atomic, and propagate cancellation.
Keep SQL and mapping tests close to the target database provider because syntax, types, casing, and query plans are provider-specific.

interviewQuestions.question: How is Dapper different from EF Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dapper maps explicit SQL over ADO.NET and provides little unit-of-work or change-tracking behavior. EF Core supplies LINQ translation, identity and change tracking, relationships, migrations, and a richer ORM model.

interviewQuestions.question: Can Dapper and EF Core be used together?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes. A common CQRS approach uses EF Core for transactional writes and Dapper for explicit read projections, provided connection and transaction ownership are coordinated when atomicity is required.

interviewQuestions.question: Does using Dapper automatically prevent SQL injection?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Dapper makes parameter binding convenient, but dynamic SQL built by concatenating untrusted input is still vulnerable. Dynamic identifiers and sort choices require allowlists.

note: Dapper reduces mapping ceremony, not the need to understand SQL, transactions, indexes, connection pooling, and provider behavior.
tip: Use a dedicated read-model type whose property names intentionally match aliased result columns.
warning: A fast mapper cannot rescue an unbounded query, missing index, long transaction, or unsafe SQL construction.
latestNote: New guide on explicit SQL, mapping, transactions, and EF Core coexistence

name: Solution Architecture Fundamentals
shortDescription: Turn business outcomes and quality requirements into explicit system boundaries, views, tradeoffs, and evolutionary decisions.
overview: Solution architecture connects business goals, stakeholder concerns, quality requirements, and constraints to a coherent design that teams can build and operate.
detail: A solution architect clarifies the problem before selecting technology. The work includes identifying stakeholders and critical flows, expressing measurable quality attributes, defining system context and boundaries, comparing architecture styles, documenting significant decisions, designing for operations and security, and validating the architecture through prototypes, reviews, tests, and production evidence. Diagrams are communication tools; the architecture is the set of decisions and constraints that shape the system throughout its life.

concepts.title: Drivers and constraints
concepts.description: Business outcomes, critical user journeys, compliance, budget, schedule, existing systems, and team capabilities define the feasible design space.

concepts.title: Quality attributes
concepts.description: Reliability, security, performance, operability, cost, and maintainability become measurable scenarios rather than vague goals.

concepts.title: Boundaries and views
concepts.description: Context, container, component, deployment, data, and runtime views explain different stakeholder concerns without one overloaded diagram.

concepts.title: Tradeoffs and evolution
concepts.description: Styles and technologies are selected against requirements, recorded as decisions, validated early, and revisited as evidence or constraints change.

architecture.description: Stakeholder outcomes and constraints shape measurable requirements, which guide architecture decisions and views that delivery teams validate through implementation and operations.

code.label: QualityScenario.cs
code.introduction: A small quality-scenario record forces an architecture requirement to name its stimulus, operating condition, expected response, and measurable target.

bestPractices: Start with business outcomes, stakeholders, critical flows, constraints, and measurable quality scenarios before choosing services or patterns.
Use a small set of complementary views and keep every diagram scoped, labeled, versioned, and connected to decisions.
Evaluate options against explicit criteria, record material tradeoffs, and prototype the assumptions with the highest cost of being wrong.
Include deployment, observability, security, data ownership, failure recovery, cost, and team ownership in the architecture from the start.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between architecture and design?
interviewQuestions.answer: Architecture focuses on system-shaping structures, constraints, quality attributes, and costly-to-reverse decisions. Design also includes the many local implementation choices made within those boundaries.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose an architecture style?
interviewQuestions.answer: Compare styles against business drivers, quality scenarios, constraints, operational model, data needs, team capabilities, and migration path; then validate the riskiest assumptions.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know an architecture is working?
interviewQuestions.answer: Define measurable fitness criteria for critical qualities, test them before release, observe them in production, review incidents and costs, and change decisions when evidence no longer supports them.

note: Architecture documentation should make important reasoning discoverable, not attempt to predict every implementation detail.
tip: Write the three most important quality scenarios and use them as evaluation criteria in every architecture review.
warning: A polished diagram without measurable requirements, ownership, tradeoffs, or validation is not an executable architecture.
latestNote: New guide on requirements, views, tradeoffs, and architecture validation

name: Architecture Decision Records
shortDescription: Capture architecturally significant choices with their context, considered options, consequences, ownership, and lifecycle.
overview: An Architecture Decision Record documents why a significant design choice was made and what consequences the team accepts.
detail: An ADR is a short, version-controlled record for a decision that shapes structure, quality attributes, constraints, or future options. It captures the context and forces, the decision, alternatives considered, expected positive and negative consequences, status, owners, and links to evidence. ADRs form a chronological decision log: accepted decisions are not silently rewritten when direction changes; a new record supersedes the old one and preserves the reasoning available at the time.

concepts.title: Architectural significance
concepts.description: Record choices that affect system structure, key qualities, organizational boundaries, or options that are expensive to reverse.

concepts.title: Context and options
concepts.description: State the problem, drivers, constraints, assumptions, and credible alternatives so the decision can be understood independently.

concepts.title: Consequences
concepts.description: Document benefits, costs, risks, operational effects, follow-up work, and the conditions that would trigger reconsideration.

concepts.title: Decision lifecycle
concepts.description: Use proposed, accepted, rejected, deprecated, and superseded states with owners, dates, and links to later decisions.

architecture.description: A significant concern is evaluated against drivers and options, accepted through review, and preserved in a versioned decision log that informs delivery and later reassessment.

code.label: docs/adr/0007-api-gateway.md
code.introduction: A compact template keeps records comparable while leaving room for evidence and explicit tradeoffs.
code.code:
# ADR-0007: Use a managed API gateway

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-08-06
- Owners: Platform Architecture

## Context
Public APIs need consistent authentication, quotas, version routing,
and telemetry across independently deployed services.

## Decision
Use Azure API Management as the external gateway.

## Alternatives
- Application-owned gateway
- Direct exposure through an ingress controller

## Consequences
Central policy and analytics improve consistency, but APIM adds cost,
latency, operational dependencies, and tier-specific constraints.

## Revisit when
Traffic, regions, or gateway availability targets materially change.

bestPractices: Keep ADRs concise, immutable after acceptance except for status and links, and store them beside the code or architecture documentation they govern.
Record only significant decisions and state the context, options, decision, consequences, owners, date, and review trigger.
Use lightweight peer review and include links to prototypes, measurements, threat models, cost estimates, and diagrams that support the choice.
Supersede an obsolete ADR with a new record instead of erasing history, and review the decision log during major changes and incidents.

interviewQuestions.question: Which decisions deserve an ADR?
interviewQuestions.answer: Decisions that materially shape the system, affect important quality attributes or organizational boundaries, impose constraints, or are difficult and expensive to reverse.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should an accepted ADR not simply be edited?
interviewQuestions.answer: Editing destroys the historical reasoning and makes it unclear what teams implemented. A superseding ADR preserves chronology while documenting the new context and decision.

interviewQuestions.question: How do ADRs avoid becoming bureaucracy?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a short template, record only significant choices, keep review close to normal code workflows, assign ownership, and link each record to delivery or validation evidence.

note: An ADR explains a decision; it does not replace diagrams, API contracts, threat models, runbooks, or implementation documentation.
tip: Start a brownfield decision log by reconstructing only the few choices currently constraining change, then record new decisions as they occur.
warning: A decision log that records only the selected option and omits context, alternatives, and consequences cannot support future reassessment.
latestNote: New guide on concise, versioned architecture decisions

name: API Design Best Practices
shortDescription: Design stable, secure, observable HTTP contracts around resources, standard semantics, compatibility, and predictable failure behavior.
overview: Good API design creates a clear, loosely coupled contract that clients can use correctly and evolve with safely.
detail: An HTTP API should model business resources and workflows rather than database tables or implementation methods. Consistent URIs, HTTP methods, status codes, media types, validation errors, pagination, filtering, concurrency controls, idempotency, asynchronous operations, versioning, security, and observability make behavior predictable. Contract-first review and compatibility tests help providers and consumers evolve independently while explicit deprecation policies prevent permanent support for accidental behavior.

concepts.title: Resource-oriented contracts
concepts.description: Stable nouns, representations, relationships, and workflow resources describe the domain without exposing internal storage or service boundaries.

concepts.title: HTTP semantics
concepts.description: Methods, safety, idempotency, status codes, headers, caching, conditional requests, and content negotiation communicate standard behavior.

concepts.title: Scale and resilience
concepts.description: Pagination, filtering, field selection, rate limits, timeouts, idempotency keys, and asynchronous operations bound work and support retries.

concepts.title: Evolution and governance
concepts.description: OpenAPI review, compatibility checks, explicit versioning, deprecation windows, security defaults, and telemetry protect clients over time.

architecture.description: Clients use a versioned contract through security and policy controls; resource handlers enforce domain rules while telemetry and compatibility checks govern evolution.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A resource endpoint uses a constrained route, typed outcomes, cancellation, and a standard validation problem response.

bestPractices: Design from consumer workflows and domain resources, publish an OpenAPI contract, and review it before implementation.
Apply standard HTTP semantics consistently, return Problem Details for machine-readable errors, and document every status and retry behavior.
Bound collections and work with pagination, filters, payload limits, quotas, timeouts, cancellation, and asynchronous patterns for long operations.
Define compatibility, versioning, deprecation, security, idempotency, concurrency, and observability policies as part of the contract.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes an HTTP operation idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Repeating the same request has the same intended effect on server state as making it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and safe retry mechanisms should respect that property even if response codes differ.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an API return 202 Accepted?
interviewQuestions.answer: When work has been accepted but will complete asynchronously. The response should identify a status resource or operation URL and document polling, completion, failure, and cancellation behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How can an API evolve without breaking clients?
interviewQuestions.answer: Prefer additive changes, tolerant readers, contract compatibility tests, explicit policies for breaking versions, usage telemetry, and a communicated deprecation window.

note: REST is one useful interaction style, not a requirement for every internal or event-driven interface; choose the style from consumer and system needs.
tip: Review a proposed API using only its OpenAPI document and example errors; hidden assumptions discovered there are cheaper to fix than deployed contracts.
warning: Exposing database tables directly couples clients to internal storage, expands the attack surface, and makes later redesign unnecessarily breaking.
latestNote: New guide on HTTP contracts, evolution, reliability, and governance

name: Multi-Tenancy Patterns
shortDescription: Balance tenant isolation, scale, cost, customization, and operations across identity, compute, data, messaging, and deployment.
overview: Multitenant architecture serves multiple customers from a solution while deliberately controlling isolation, scale, cost, performance, and customization.
detail: Multitenancy is not one binary infrastructure choice. Each component can be pooled, partitioned, stamped, or dedicated according to data sensitivity, performance, geography, commercial tier, and operational requirements. Tenant identity must be derived from trusted authentication context and enforced through every data and cache path. A control plane automates onboarding, placement, configuration, lifecycle, and metering while quotas, partitioning, observability, and tests protect tenants from leakage and noisy neighbors.

concepts.title: Isolation models
concepts.description: Shared, partitioned, deployment-stamp, and dedicated models trade cost and density against security, performance, customization, and operational independence.

concepts.title: Tenant context
concepts.description: Trusted identity claims establish tenant context, which authorization, routing, data filters, cache keys, logs, metrics, and messages must propagate safely.

concepts.title: Control plane
concepts.description: Automated onboarding, provisioning, placement, configuration, billing, offboarding, and capacity management keep tenant lifecycle work repeatable.

concepts.title: Scale and fairness
concepts.description: Quotas, rate limits, partition keys, workload isolation, capacity signals, and per-tenant telemetry contain noisy neighbors and support service tiers.

architecture.description: Trusted identity establishes tenant context at the edge, a control plane manages placement and lifecycle, and isolated data-plane stamps serve tenant traffic with per-tenant policy and telemetry.

code.label: TenantContextMiddleware.cs
code.introduction: Tenant context is derived from an authenticated claim and stored in a scoped service instead of trusting a caller-supplied tenant header.

bestPractices: Define isolation, residency, performance, recovery, customization, and commercial requirements per component before choosing a tenancy model.
Derive tenant context from authenticated identity, authorize it centrally, and include it in every query, cache key, event, job, log, and metric.
Automate onboarding, provisioning, placement, migration, metering, suspension, and deletion through an idempotent control plane.
Test cross-tenant access, cache separation, noisy-neighbor limits, stamp failure, tenant migration, and offboarding with production-shaped scale.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the main multitenancy isolation models?
interviewQuestions.answer: Resources can be fully shared, logically partitioned, grouped into deployment stamps, or dedicated per tenant. Real solutions often mix models by tier and component.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you prevent cross-tenant data leakage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Establish tenant identity from trusted authentication, enforce authorization and tenant filters at multiple layers, partition data deliberately, scope caches and messages, and run automated negative isolation tests.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a multitenant control plane solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It automates tenant lifecycle and infrastructure management, including onboarding, provisioning, configuration, placement, scaling, metering, migration, suspension, and deletion.

note: A product can be multitenant at the business layer while using a mixture of shared and dedicated infrastructure underneath.
tip: Create a component-by-component tenancy matrix showing isolation, scale unit, data boundary, failure blast radius, and cost owner.
warning: Never authorize a tenant solely from an unverified request header, route value, or query parameter supplied by the caller.
latestNote: New guide on SaaS isolation, tenant context, control planes, and scale

name: Saga Pattern
shortDescription: Coordinate distributed business transactions as local commits with durable progress, idempotent messages, and explicit compensation.
overview: The Saga pattern maintains business consistency across independently owned services by coordinating local transactions and compensating completed work when later steps fail.
detail: A saga decomposes a distributed workflow into local transactions. Each successful step durably records its state and triggers the next action through a command or event. Failures invoke business-specific compensating actions where reversal is possible. Choreography distributes coordination across event handlers; orchestration gives one durable coordinator an explicit state machine. Both require idempotency, duplicate handling, correlation, timeouts, retries, observability, and reconciliation because messages and failures can occur at any boundary.

concepts.title: Local transactions
concepts.description: Each participant commits only its own data and publishes progress reliably, commonly through a transactional outbox.

concepts.title: Compensation and pivot
concepts.description: Compensable steps have semantic undo actions; the pivot is the point after which the remaining retryable steps must complete.

concepts.title: Orchestration or choreography
concepts.description: An orchestrator centralizes workflow state, while choreography reacts to events with less central control but harder end-to-end visibility.

concepts.title: Delivery correctness
concepts.description: Correlation IDs, idempotent handlers, inbox or deduplication state, retries, timeouts, ordering rules, and reconciliation make at-least-once delivery safe.

architecture.description: A durable saga state coordinates commands to service-owned local transactions; replies advance the workflow, while failures trigger compensation and telemetry supports reconciliation.

code.label: PlaceOrderSaga.cs
code.introduction: An explicit state record makes successful steps and compensation progress durable and safe to retry.

bestPractices: Model the workflow, invariants, compensable actions, pivot, retryable actions, timeouts, and terminal states explicitly with domain owners.
Persist saga progress durably and use transactional outbox and inbox or deduplication mechanisms for reliable, idempotent message handling.
Give every saga and message correlation and causation identifiers, structured telemetry, deadlines, and an operator-visible reconciliation path.
Test duplicate, delayed, reordered, lost, and poison messages plus compensation failure and coordinator restart before production.

interviewQuestions.question: How is saga choreography different from orchestration?
interviewQuestions.answer: Choreography has participants react to events without one coordinator. Orchestration uses a central state machine that commands steps and handles replies, improving visibility but concentrating workflow coupling.

interviewQuestions.question: Is a compensating action the same as a database rollback?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Compensation is a new business operation that semantically offsets a committed action; it may be partial, fail independently, require approval, or be impossible after a pivot.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must saga handlers be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Brokers and retries commonly produce duplicate delivery. Idempotent handlers ensure processing the same message again does not repeat charges, reservations, or other side effects.

note: A saga provides eventual business consistency, not ACID isolation across services; users and downstream processes may observe intermediate states.
tip: Draw the happy path and every compensation in one state-transition diagram before implementing handlers.
warning: Do not describe a chain of best-effort HTTP calls as a saga unless workflow state, recovery, idempotency, and compensation are durable and explicit.
latestNote: New standalone guide on distributed workflow consistency and compensation

name: Legacy Modernization
shortDescription: Modernize applications incrementally through portfolio assessment, rationalization, strangler delivery, data transition, and measurable outcomes.
overview: Legacy modernization improves business value and system qualities through evidence-based portfolio decisions and controlled, incremental change.
detail: Modernization begins with business outcomes, portfolio inventory, dependency discovery, risk, cost, and operational evidence. Each workload or capability can be retained, retired, rehosted, replatformed, refactored, or rebuilt rather than receiving one strategy for the entire estate. Incremental patterns such as strangler routing, anti-corruption layers, change-data capture, parallel runs, and reversible cutovers reduce migration risk while automated tests and observability create a safety net.

concepts.title: Assessment and outcomes
concepts.description: Inventory applications, dependencies, ownership, costs, risks, usage, data, and quality gaps, then define measurable business outcomes.

concepts.title: Rationalization strategies
concepts.description: Retain, retire, rehost, replatform, refactor, and rebuild decisions are applied per workload or capability using value, risk, and feasibility.

concepts.title: Incremental replacement
concepts.description: Strangler routing and anti-corruption adapters let new capabilities replace bounded legacy behavior without a single big-bang cutover.

concepts.title: Data and operating transition
concepts.description: Data ownership, synchronization, reconciliation, observability, support, rollback, and team skills are migrated alongside application code.

architecture.description: A routing facade directs selected capabilities to modern services while an anti-corruption layer protects the new model and synchronized data enables gradual, observable cutover.

code.label: LegacyCustomerAdapter.cs
code.introduction: An anti-corruption adapter translates a legacy contract into the new domain vocabulary and prevents old representations from spreading.

bestPractices: Define business outcomes and baseline cost, reliability, security, delivery, performance, and usage before selecting a modernization strategy.
Map dependencies and data ownership, then modernize bounded capabilities in thin, reversible slices with explicit exit and rollback criteria.
Build characterization tests, contract tests, telemetry, reconciliation, and parallel-run evidence before redirecting critical traffic.
Plan operating model, skills, security, compliance, support, decommissioning, and data retention as first-class parts of the program.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose among modernization strategies?
interviewQuestions.answer: Assess business value, urgency, technical health, dependencies, risk, compliance, cost, team skills, target qualities, and migration feasibility per workload or capability.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Strangler Fig pattern?
interviewQuestions.answer: A facade gradually routes selected capabilities from a legacy system to new implementations until the old behavior can be safely retired.

interviewQuestions.question: Why do modernization programs fail despite new technology?
interviewQuestions.answer: Common causes include unclear outcomes, hidden dependencies, big-bang scope, weak test and telemetry safety nets, ignored data migration, unchanged operating practices, and no funded decommissioning.

note: Modernization can improve the existing system in place; migration to a public cloud is one option, not the definition of modernization.
tip: Choose one valuable, weakly coupled capability and prove the assessment-to-cutover path before scaling the program.
warning: A rewrite that preserves unclear requirements, coupling, data problems, and operating practices can recreate the legacy system on a newer stack.
latestNote: New guide on assessment, 6 Rs, strangler delivery, and safe cutover

name: Azure Resource Manager
shortDescription: Govern Azure infrastructure through a unified management layer — resource groups, subscriptions, RBAC, policies, locks, and deployment modes.
overview: Azure Resource Manager is the control plane for all Azure resources — every portal click, CLI command, Bicep deployment, and SDK call goes through ARM, which enforces identity, policy, and governance before any resource is touched.
detail: ARM provides a consistent management layer across all Azure services. It organises resources into a hierarchy — management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resources — and applies access control, policy, tags, and locks at any level of that hierarchy. Understanding ARM is fundamental to architect-level Azure work because governance decisions made at the ARM layer affect every team and every workload in a tenant. Deployment modes, resource providers, the management plane versus data plane distinction, and the ARM REST API underpin every IaC tool including Bicep, Terraform, and Pulumi.

concepts.title: Resource hierarchy
concepts.description: Resources live in resource groups, resource groups live in subscriptions, and subscriptions live in management groups. Policies and RBAC assignments at a higher scope inherit down, enabling consistent governance across all workloads.

concepts.title: RBAC and role assignments
concepts.description: Azure RBAC controls who can perform which actions on which resources using built-in and custom role definitions assigned to users, groups, service principals, or managed identities at any scope in the hierarchy.

concepts.title: Azure Policy
concepts.description: Policies define rules that ARM evaluates on every resource write — preventing non-compliant resources from being created, auditing existing ones, or automatically remediating drift from the desired configuration baseline.

concepts.title: Deployment modes and resource locks
concepts.description: Incremental mode adds or updates resources without touching others in the group; complete mode deletes any resource not in the template. Resource locks — CanNotDelete and ReadOnly — prevent accidental or unauthorised changes outside the deployment pipeline.

architecture.description: Every Azure operation — portal, CLI, SDK, or IaC — passes through the ARM API, which authenticates via Entra ID, evaluates RBAC and Policy, and routes to the target resource provider.

code.label: ArmGovernance.cs
code.introduction: The Azure SDK for .NET manages ARM-level resources — creating resource groups, assigning roles, and applying locks — directly in code for automation pipelines or custom governance tooling.

bestPractices: Design the management group and subscription hierarchy before deploying workloads — retrofitting governance scope after resources exist is significantly more complex and disruptive.
Assign Azure roles at the narrowest practical scope—usually a subscription or resource group—and reserve management-group assignments for genuinely shared platform responsibilities.
Use Azure Policy deny effects for non-negotiable standards — allowed locations, required tags, SKU restrictions — and audit effects for visibility before escalating to deny.
Apply CanNotDelete locks to production resource groups containing stateful resources so accidental complete-mode deployments or manual deletions require an explicit lock removal step.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the management plane and the data plane in Azure?
interviewQuestions.answer: The management plane is the ARM API used to create, update, delete, and configure resources — all RBAC and Policy enforcement happens here. The data plane is the resource's own API for working with its content — reading blobs from Storage, sending messages to Service Bus, or querying a database. A user can have ARM RBAC rights to manage a resource without having data plane access to its content, and vice versa.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between incremental and complete deployment mode?
interviewQuestions.answer: Incremental mode, the recommended default, adds or updates resources in the template while leaving unspecified resources in place. Complete mode deletes resources that are absent from the template, but Microsoft is gradually deprecating it for deletion scenarios; use deployment stacks when a declarative deployment must also remove resources.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you enforce a tagging standard across all resources in an Azure tenant?
interviewQuestions.answer: Assign an Azure Policy at the management group scope with a deny effect that requires specified tag keys on all resource writes. For existing untagged resources, use a modify policy with a remediation task to apply default tag values. This ensures compliance for new resources immediately and provides a path to remediate existing ones.

note: ARM governance decisions — hierarchy design, policy scope, RBAC model — are very difficult to change after workloads are deployed. Treat the ARM layer as foundational architecture that deserves the same design rigour as application architecture.
tip: Use the Azure Resource Graph to query the live state of all resources across subscriptions using KQL — it is far faster than iterating through the ARM SDK and essential for compliance reporting and cost visibility at scale.
warning: Complete deployment mode deletes resources that are absent from the template and is not recommended for new deletion workflows. Prefer deployment stacks, and always review a what-if result before any potentially destructive deployment.
latestNote: New guide on ARM hierarchy, RBAC, Azure Policy, deployment modes, and resource locks

name: Azure API Management
shortDescription: Publish, secure, transform, observe, and govern APIs through a managed gateway, control plane, developer experience, and policy model.
overview: Azure API Management is a managed platform for exposing and governing APIs across Azure, on-premises, hybrid, and multicloud environments.
detail: API Management separates the gateway data plane from the management plane used to configure APIs, products, subscriptions, policies, analytics, and the developer portal. The gateway routes requests, validates credentials, enforces quotas and rate limits, transforms messages, caches selected responses, and emits telemetry. Architecture choices include service tier, regional deployment, network connectivity, gateway availability, self-hosted gateways, policy scope, backend resilience, secret management, and disaster recovery.

concepts.title: Gateway data plane
concepts.description: The managed or self-hosted gateway proxies traffic, authenticates callers, applies policies, routes to backends, and emits runtime telemetry.

concepts.title: Management plane
concepts.description: APIs, operations, products, subscriptions, named values, versions, revisions, workspaces, and policies define the governed API lifecycle.

concepts.title: Policy pipeline
concepts.description: Inbound, backend, outbound, and on-error policies compose authentication, transformation, caching, quotas, routing, and failure behavior.

concepts.title: Reliability and topology
concepts.description: Tier capabilities, zones, regions, networking, capacity, backend health, deployment automation, and recovery targets shape production design.

architecture.description: Consumers call an APIM gateway that applies identity and traffic policies, routes to protected backend APIs, and exports telemetry while the management plane controls configuration.

code.label: inbound-policy.xml
code.introduction: An inbound policy validates an Entra-issued JWT, limits calls per authenticated subject, and adds a correlation identifier before forwarding the request.
code.code:
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401">
      <openid-config url="{{entra-openid-config}}" />
      <audiences><audience>{{orders-api-audience}}</audience></audiences>
    </validate-jwt>
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="120" renewal-period="60"
      counter-key="@(context.Principal?.Identity?.Name ?? context.Request.IpAddress)" />
    <set-header name="x-correlation-id" exists-action="skip">
      <value>@(context.RequestId.ToString())</value>
    </set-header>
  </inbound>
  <backend><base /></backend>
  <outbound><base /></outbound>
  <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>

bestPractices: Select a tier and topology from required capacity, availability zones or regions, private connectivity, certificates, self-hosting, and recovery objectives.
Keep policies small, scoped, version-controlled, tested, and deployed through infrastructure as code; use named values backed by Key Vault for secrets.
Authenticate callers and backends, allowlist exposure, bound payloads and rates, and avoid treating subscription keys as user authorization.
Monitor gateway capacity, latency, failures, policy errors, backend health, quotas, certificates, and regional behavior with actionable ownership.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the APIM gateway and management plane?
interviewQuestions.answer: The gateway is the runtime data plane that processes API traffic and policies. The management plane configures APIs, products, subscriptions, policies, users, and operational settings.

interviewQuestions.question: Where should authentication and authorization happen with APIM?
interviewQuestions.answer: APIM can validate tokens and enforce coarse API policy, while backends should still enforce resource and domain authorization. The gateway must not become the only trust boundary.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you design APIM for high availability?
interviewQuestions.answer: Match service tier and deployment to zone and region targets, design backend and DNS failover, automate configuration, monitor capacity and certificates, and test gateway and dependency failure paths.

note: API Management governs API exposure; it does not replace careful API contract design, backend authorization, service resilience, or lifecycle ownership.
tip: Treat every APIM policy as production code with source control, review, automated deployment, test calls, and observability.
warning: Tier capabilities and networking behavior differ materially; validate current limits and availability features before committing an architecture.
latestNote: New guide on managed gateways, policies, security, and topology

name: Azure Functions & Serverless
shortDescription: Build event-driven .NET workloads with triggers, bindings, isolated workers, elastic hosting, durable workflows, and production-safe operations.
overview: Azure Functions runs event-driven code on managed, elastic compute and integrates .NET handlers with HTTP, schedules, queues, streams, storage, and other services.
detail: A function app groups functions that share deployment, configuration, scaling, and hosting. Triggers start executions and bindings integrate data, while the .NET isolated worker uses the standard hosting and dependency-injection model outside the Functions host process. Hosting plan, scale behavior, cold starts, concurrency, retries, poison handling, idempotency, networking, identity, observability, package deployment, and execution duration all affect whether a serverless design meets its workload goals.

concepts.title: Triggers and bindings
concepts.description: One trigger starts a function; input and output bindings connect supported services, while SDK clients handle advanced operations explicitly.

concepts.title: .NET isolated worker
concepts.description: A separate .NET process provides modern target-framework control, middleware, dependency injection, configuration, and familiar hosting patterns.

concepts.title: Hosting and scale
concepts.description: Flex Consumption, Premium, dedicated, and container options differ in scale, networking, cold-start, duration, instance, and cost behavior.

concepts.title: Delivery correctness
concepts.description: At-least-once events require idempotency, retry policies, poison handling, checkpoint awareness, correlation, and durable workflow state.

architecture.description: Events enter through Functions triggers, isolated .NET workers execute stateless handlers and call managed dependencies, while durable state, retries, and telemetry support reliable scale.

code.label: CreateOrderFunction.cs
code.introduction: An isolated-worker HTTP function uses constructor injection, structured logging, cancellation, and an explicit response contract.

bestPractices: Use the .NET isolated worker for new C# function apps, pin supported runtime and extension versions, and automate infrastructure and package deployment.
Design event handlers as idempotent operations with bounded retries, poison-message handling, timeouts, cancellation, and correlation.
Choose hosting from measured latency, scale, networking, duration, concurrency, availability, and cost requirements rather than the serverless label alone.
Use managed identity, least privilege, centralized configuration, OpenTelemetry or Application Insights, health signals, and production-shaped load tests.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the .NET isolated worker model?
interviewQuestions.answer: Function code runs in a separate .NET process from the Functions host, enabling independent framework targeting and familiar dependency injection, middleware, configuration, and hosting patterns.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must queue-triggered functions be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event delivery and retries can invoke a handler more than once. Idempotency prevents duplicate charges, writes, notifications, or other side effects.

interviewQuestions.question: When might Azure Functions be the wrong compute choice?
interviewQuestions.answer: When workloads need highly predictable always-warm latency, unusual host control, very long or specialized compute, incompatible networking, or a stable load whose economics favor another hosting model.

note: Serverless transfers server management and scaling responsibilities; it does not remove capacity limits, distributed-systems behavior, security, or operations.
tip: Load test cold and warm executions with real bindings and observe instance scale, dependency pressure, retries, and end-to-end latency.
warning: Do not assume exactly-once event delivery; build handlers and downstream effects to tolerate duplicates and partial failure.
latestNote: New guide on isolated workers, event delivery, hosting, and scale

name: Azure Logic Apps
shortDescription: Automate enterprise workflows and system integrations using Azure Logic Apps — connecting hundreds of services with triggers, actions, and conditional logic without writing infrastructure code.
overview: Azure Logic Apps is a cloud platform for building and running automated workflows that integrate applications, data, services, and systems across an enterprise with minimal code.
detail: Logic Apps uses a visual designer backed by a JSON workflow definition to connect triggers—such as a Service Bus message, HTTP request, schedule, or arriving file—to actions from a large catalog of built-in and managed connectors. A Standard logic app runs in the single-tenant Azure Logic Apps runtime, can host multiple stateful or stateless workflows, and supports local development, private networking, and dedicated plan-based billing. Consumption is multitenant, hosts one stateful workflow per app, and bills per execution. A separate hybrid option can host the Standard runtime on your infrastructure through an Azure Container Apps extension. Logic Apps fits scenarios where integration workflow and connector orchestration outweigh custom computation.

concepts.title: Triggers and connectors
concepts.description: A trigger starts a workflow — on a schedule, on a message arrival, on an HTTP call, or on a change in an external system. Connectors provide pre-built authenticated integrations to hundreds of services without managing credentials or SDKs.

concepts.title: Stateful vs stateless workflows
concepts.description: Stateful workflows persist run history and intermediate state to storage, enabling long-running orchestrations, human approvals, and retry inspection. Stateless workflows keep state in memory only, offering lower latency for short-lived, high-frequency integrations.

concepts.title: Standard vs Consumption tier
concepts.description: Consumption Logic Apps run in the multitenant service and bill per trigger and action execution. Standard Logic Apps use the single-tenant runtime and a plan-based model, supporting private networking, local development, and multiple stateful or stateless workflows in one app.

concepts.title: Integration accounts and B2B
concepts.description: An Integration Account stores EDI schemas, maps, trading partner agreements, and certificates, enabling Logic Apps to process AS2, EDIFACT, and X12 messages for B2B integrations — a capability that would require significant custom code to replicate.

architecture.description: A trigger fires the workflow; each action calls a connector or runs inline code; the workflow state is persisted between steps for long-running orchestrations and surfaced in the run history for monitoring.

code.label: OrderWorkflowClient.cs
code.introduction: Logic Apps workflows are JSON definitions — this excerpt shows an HTTP trigger, a Service Bus send action, and a conditional branch, the same structure visible in the visual designer.

bestPractices: Use Logic Apps for integration orchestration and connector-heavy workflows; use Azure Functions or .NET Workers for compute-heavy, latency-sensitive, or complex business logic that needs unit testing and version control.
Store sensitive workflow inputs and connector credentials as Logic Apps parameters backed by Key Vault references — never hardcode connection strings or API keys in the workflow definition.
Design long-running approval workflows as stateful workflows with explicit timeout and cancellation branches so workflows do not run indefinitely when an approver is unavailable.
Version workflow definitions in source control and deploy via CI/CD using the Azure CLI or Bicep — treat the JSON definition as infrastructure code rather than a designer-only artefact.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Logic Apps over Azure Functions for an integration scenario?
interviewQuestions.answer: Logic Apps is the right choice when the integration is connector-heavy — Office 365, Salesforce, SAP, EDI — and the orchestration logic is conditional branching, looping, and sequencing rather than complex computation. Functions are better when the logic requires unit testing, custom algorithms, precise latency control, or dependencies not available as connectors.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Standard and Consumption Logic Apps?
interviewQuestions.answer: Consumption Logic Apps are multitenant, pay-per-execution resources that host one stateful workflow per app. Standard Logic Apps use the single-tenant runtime and a plan-based model, host multiple stateful or stateless workflows, support local development and private networking, and can also use a separate hybrid hosting option backed by an Azure Container Apps extension.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle errors and retries in a Logic Apps workflow?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each action in a Logic Apps workflow can be configured with a retry policy — fixed or exponential backoff with a configurable count and interval. Run-after conditions on subsequent actions determine whether they execute on success, failure, timeout, or skipped status of the preceding action, enabling branching error-handling logic without custom exception handling code.

note: Logic Apps excels at enterprise integration patterns — it is not a general application platform. Workflows with significant business logic, custom data transformations, or testing requirements are better served by .NET code.
tip: Use the Standard tier with local development tooling for any workflow that will be maintained long-term — it enables debugging in VS Code, source-controlled workflow definitions, and deployment through standard Azure pipelines.
warning: Consumption Logic Apps can accumulate significant costs under high-volume scenarios where thousands of actions execute per minute — model expected execution counts before choosing the consumption tier for frequent event-driven workflows.
latestNote: New guide on triggers, connectors, stateful workflows, Standard vs Consumption, and B2B integration

name: Azure Event Hubs
shortDescription: Ingest millions of events per second into Azure using Event Hubs — a fully managed, Kafka-compatible streaming platform with partitioned consumers, capture, and schema registry.
overview: Azure Event Hubs is a fully managed big-data streaming platform that can receive and process millions of events per second with low latency, offering Kafka protocol compatibility and deep Azure ecosystem integration.
detail: Event Hubs acts as the front door for event pipelines — telemetry ingestion, clickstream data, IoT device events, and application logs flow in through producers and are processed by consumers reading partitioned streams at their own pace. The EventProcessorClient in the Azure SDK for .NET handles partition ownership, checkpointing to Azure Blob Storage, and load-balanced consumption across multiple instances. Event Hubs is Kafka protocol-compatible, so existing Confluent.Kafka clients work by changing only the bootstrap server. Event Hubs Capture writes the stream to Azure Data Lake or Blob Storage in Avro format for batch analytics without additional pipeline code.

concepts.title: Partitions and throughput units
concepts.description: Events are distributed across partitions for parallel processing. Throughput units — or processing units in Premium — control ingress and egress capacity. Partition count is fixed at creation and determines maximum consumer parallelism.

concepts.title: EventProcessorClient and checkpointing
concepts.description: EventProcessorClient distributes partition ownership across multiple instances, processes events in batches, and persists checkpoints to Azure Blob Storage so processing resumes from the last committed offset after a restart.

concepts.title: Kafka compatibility
concepts.description: Event Hubs exposes a Kafka endpoint on port 9093. Confluent.Kafka and MassTransit Kafka transport clients connect by replacing the bootstrap server with the Event Hubs namespace FQDN and using a connection string as the SASL password.

concepts.title: Event Hubs Capture
concepts.description: Capture automatically writes the event stream to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake in Avro format on a time or size interval — enabling batch analytics, archiving, and event replay without any pipeline code.

architecture.description: Producers send events to Event Hubs partitions; EventProcessorClient instances compete for partition ownership and checkpoint progress to Blob Storage; Capture writes the stream to Data Lake for batch consumers.

code.label: OrderEventProcessor.cs
code.introduction: EventProcessorClient handles partition ownership and checkpoint coordination. This simple handler processes one event at a time and checkpoints only after success; high-throughput applications should checkpoint at a deliberate interval rather than writing a checkpoint for every event.

bestPractices: Checkpoint only after successful processing, and choose a bounded checkpoint cadence—checkpointing every event increases storage operations, while checkpointing too rarely increases replay after failure.
Size partition count to match expected peak consumer instances — you cannot increase parallelism beyond the partition count regardless of how many processor instances you run.

Enable Event Hubs Capture from the start for production streams — it provides a zero-code archiving and replay capability that is very difficult to add retroactively once the retention window has passed.
Use managed identity for both producers and the EventProcessorClient in production — connection strings in configuration are a rotation burden and a security risk; managed identity eliminates both.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the role of checkpointing in Event Hubs processing?
interviewQuestions.answer: Checkpointing persists the offset of the last successfully processed event for each partition to Azure Blob Storage. When a processor instance restarts or another instance takes over a partition, it reads the checkpoint and resumes from where processing left off rather than from the beginning of the stream or the latest event.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Event Hubs over Azure Service Bus?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event Hubs is designed for high-throughput event streaming — telemetry, logs, IoT, clickstreams — where multiple consumers read the same stream independently and ordering within a partition matters. Service Bus is designed for reliable message queuing and task distribution with dead-lettering, sessions, deferral, and transactional sends. Use Event Hubs for streaming analytics pipelines; use Service Bus for business process messaging and command distribution.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Event Hubs Kafka compatibility work and what are its limits?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event Hubs exposes the Kafka protocol over TLS on port 9093, using SASL_SSL with Microsoft Entra OAuth or SAS authentication. Kafka topics map to event hubs, while partitions and offsets map directly. Event Hubs remains a managed service that scales through throughput or processing units; some Kafka capabilities, including transactions and Kafka Streams, are tier-dependent previews in Premium and Dedicated.

note: Event Hubs retention is time-based, not consumption-based — events are deleted after the configured retention period regardless of whether they were consumed. Design consumer catch-up strategies and use Capture for long-term archiving.
tip: Use the Kafka-compatible endpoint when migrating existing Kafka producers from a self-managed cluster to Event Hubs — change only the bootstrap server and credential configuration, validate, then decommission the cluster.
warning: Event Hubs provides at-least-once delivery. A failure after a side effect but before the next checkpoint can replay events, so handlers and downstream writes must be idempotent even though partition ownership is coordinated between processor instances.
latestNote: New guide on partitions, EventProcessorClient, checkpointing, Kafka compatibility, and Capture

name: Azure Data Factory & ETL
shortDescription: Orchestrate secure batch data movement and transformation through pipelines, activities, datasets, linked services, and integration runtimes.
overview: Azure Data Factory is a managed data-integration service for orchestrating movement and transformation across cloud and on-premises data stores.
detail: ADF pipelines group activities into repeatable workflows. Linked services define connections, datasets describe data shape or location, and integration runtimes provide movement, activity dispatch, and SSIS execution across network boundaries. Copy activity moves data; mapping data flows and external compute perform transformations. Parameters, metadata-driven patterns, triggers, incremental watermarks, managed identity, Key Vault, monitoring, retries, validation, and reconciliation make pipelines maintainable at scale. New analytics programs should also evaluate Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric while existing ADF workloads remain supported.

concepts.title: Pipeline orchestration
concepts.description: Pipelines compose copy, transformation, control-flow, notebook, stored-procedure, and custom activities with dependencies and parameters.

concepts.title: Connections and data
concepts.description: Linked services describe connection information while datasets identify the input and output data used by activities.

concepts.title: Integration runtime
concepts.description: Azure, self-hosted, and Azure-SSIS runtimes provide compute and network reach for data movement, activity dispatch, and package execution.

concepts.title: Incremental reliability
concepts.description: Watermarks, change tracking, partitioning, retries, idempotent sinks, validation, lineage, alerts, and reconciliation support repeatable ingestion.

architecture.description: Triggers start parameterized ADF pipelines, an integration runtime reaches source systems, activities move or transform data, and validated results land in governed analytical storage.

code.label: pipeline-copy-orders.json
code.introduction: A parameterized Copy activity passes a watermark to the source dataset and writes through a configured sink dataset.

bestPractices: Use metadata-driven, parameterized pipelines and reusable datasets or linked services instead of cloning environment-specific workflows.
Prefer managed identity, Key Vault references, private connectivity where required, least privilege, and a self-hosted runtime only when network reach demands it.
Design incremental loads with durable watermarks, idempotent sinks, partitioning, schema handling, validation, reconciliation, and replay procedures.
Deploy through source control and CI/CD, separate environments, monitor activity and data-quality outcomes, and track lineage, throughput, retries, and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an integration runtime in Azure Data Factory?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is the compute and network bridge used for data movement, dispatching supported activities, transformations, and SSIS execution. Azure, self-hosted, and Azure-SSIS types serve different needs.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
interviewQuestions.answer: ETL transforms data before loading the target. ELT loads data first and uses the target analytical engine for transformation; the best choice depends on scale, governance, latency, and engine capabilities.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you make an incremental pipeline restartable?
interviewQuestions.answer: Persist a committed watermark separately from in-flight work, make writes idempotent or transactional, partition work, validate counts and quality, and advance the watermark only after successful reconciliation.

note: ADF is primarily an orchestration and integration service; complex transformations may be better executed by specialized engines it coordinates.
tip: Track both pipeline success and data correctness—row counts, freshness, schema, duplicates, and reconciliation can fail independently of activity status.
warning: Never advance an incremental watermark before the target write and validation are durably complete, or failed data can be skipped permanently.
latestNote: New guide on pipelines, integration runtimes, incremental ETL, and operations

name: Cloud Adoption Framework
shortDescription: Align Azure adoption with business outcomes through strategy, planning, landing zones, workload adoption, governance, security, and management.
overview: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework provides an organization-wide roadmap for adopting Azure and integrating it into business, platform, governance, security, and operations.
detail: CAF organizes cloud adoption into connected methodologies. Strategy defines motivations and outcomes; Plan prepares people, skills, inventory, costs, and a roadmap; Ready establishes the Azure environment and landing zones; Adopt migrates, modernizes, or builds cloud-native workloads. Govern, Secure, and Manage operate continuously across the estate. CAF complements the workload-focused Well-Architected Framework and implementation patterns in the Azure Architecture Center.

concepts.title: Strategy and Plan
concepts.description: Business outcomes, financial justification, operating model, skills, digital estate, prioritization, and an actionable adoption backlog set direction.

concepts.title: Ready and landing zones
concepts.description: Tenant, identity, management groups, subscriptions, networking, policy, security, and platform automation create a governed environment for workloads.

concepts.title: Adopt workloads
concepts.description: Teams choose migration, modernization, or cloud-native paths and onboard workloads through repeatable application landing zones and delivery practices.

concepts.title: Govern, Secure, and Manage
concepts.description: Continuous controls, security posture, operations, cost, compliance, ownership, and improvement keep the cloud estate aligned as it grows.

architecture.description: Business strategy becomes an adoption plan and landing-zone foundation; workload teams then migrate or build while governance, security, and management operate continuously across the estate.

code.label: application-landing-zone.bicep
code.introduction: A small application landing-zone module exposes ownership and environment metadata as required deployment inputs instead of adding them manually later.

bestPractices: Tie adoption to measurable business outcomes, named owners, funding, risk, and an operating model rather than a technology migration target alone.
Use enterprise-scale landing-zone principles but tailor implementation to organizational size, compliance, connectivity, and platform capabilities.
Automate subscription and application landing-zone vending, policy, identity, networking, budgets, observability, and workload onboarding as platform products.
Run Govern, Secure, and Manage continuously, and assess individual workloads with the Well-Architected Framework throughout their lifecycle.

interviewQuestions.question: How is CAF different from the Azure Well-Architected Framework?
interviewQuestions.answer: CAF guides organization-wide cloud adoption, platform readiness, governance, security, and management. WAF evaluates the design and operation of individual workloads across five quality pillars.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an Azure landing zone?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a scalable, governed Azure environment and operating foundation covering identity, resource organization, subscriptions, networking, policy, security, management, and automation for workload onboarding.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are Govern, Secure, and Manage continuous?
interviewQuestions.answer: The estate, threats, regulations, costs, services, and workloads keep changing, so controls and operations must evolve throughout adoption rather than occur once at the end.

note: CAF is adaptable guidance, not a mandate to implement every enterprise control before the first workload can learn and deliver value.
tip: Map each CAF methodology to a concrete outcome, accountable team, evidence artifact, and next review date.
warning: A landing zone built without an adoption backlog and workload-team feedback can become an expensive platform with no successful consumers.
latestNote: New guide on cloud strategy, landing zones, adoption, and operations

name: AWS for .NET
shortDescription: Build and operate .NET workloads on AWS with the SDK, dependency injection, identity roles, managed compute, observability, and infrastructure as code.
overview: .NET applications can use AWS SDK clients and managed services across serverless, containers, web hosting, data, messaging, observability, and infrastructure automation.
detail: The AWS SDK for .NET provides service clients, credential and region resolution, retries, pagination, waiters, and dependency-injection integrations. Workloads can run on Lambda, App Runner, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, EKS, EC2, or other compute selected from latency, scaling, control, networking, and cost needs. IAM roles and temporary credentials, Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry, resilient SDK configuration, infrastructure as code, and multi-account governance form the production foundation.

concepts.title: SDK clients
concepts.description: Service-specific clients expose AWS APIs with asynchronous calls, pagination, retries, region selection, credential resolution, and configurable HTTP behavior.

concepts.title: Compute choices
concepts.description: Lambda, App Runner, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, EKS, and EC2 trade operational control, scale behavior, startup, portability, networking, and cost.

concepts.title: Identity and configuration
concepts.description: IAM roles, temporary credentials, least privilege, workload identity, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, and KMS avoid embedded long-lived secrets.

concepts.title: Operations and delivery
concepts.description: CloudWatch, OpenTelemetry, health checks, deployment strategies, CDK or CloudFormation, tagging, budgets, and multi-account boundaries support production.

architecture.description: A .NET workload obtains temporary role credentials, calls AWS services through reusable SDK clients, and emits correlated telemetry while infrastructure and policy are deployed as code.

code.label: DocumentStore.cs
code.introduction: A reusable S3 client relies on the default AWS credential and region chain, allowing local profiles and deployed IAM roles without secrets in code.

bestPractices: Use IAM roles and temporary credentials with least-privilege policies; never embed access keys in source, images, logs, or application settings.
