Reuse injected SDK clients, propagate cancellation, configure timeouts and retries deliberately, paginate results, and make retried side effects idempotent.
Choose compute and data services from workload requirements, team capabilities, recovery targets, networking, portability, and measured total cost.
Deploy accounts, networks, policy, alarms, dashboards, budgets, and application infrastructure as code with tags and tested rollback or roll-forward paths.

interviewQuestions.question: How does the AWS SDK for .NET find credentials?
interviewQuestions.answer: It follows a credential provider chain that can use explicit configuration, environment sources, local shared profiles, and workload role credentials. Production workloads should normally use temporary IAM role credentials.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Lambda versus ECS for a .NET workload?
interviewQuestions.answer: Lambda suits event-driven, bounded executions with elastic demand and minimal host management. ECS suits longer-running services, custom containers, steady processes, and workloads needing more control over runtime and networking.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a .NET service handle AWS API throttling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use SDK retry behavior with bounded backoff and jitter, respect cancellation and timeouts, reduce concurrency or batch requests, monitor quotas, and ensure retried mutations are idempotent.

note: The AWS SDK for .NET is independent of the compute host; the same application can call AWS services from AWS, on-premises, another cloud, or local development when identity and networking permit.
tip: Test locally with a named profile, but deploy with an IAM role and verify the exact permissions through an integration test in a nonproduction account.
warning: Do not rely on broad managed IAM policies for convenience in production; scope actions and resources and monitor denied access while refining least privilege.
latestNote: New guide on AWS SDK clients, compute, IAM, observability, and delivery

name: Azure Container Apps
shortDescription: Run containerised .NET workloads on serverless infrastructure with built-in scaling, service discovery, Dapr, and .NET Aspire integration.
overview: Azure Container Apps runs containers on fully managed infrastructure, handling scaling, service discovery, ingress, certificates, and revision traffic-splitting without exposing Kubernetes cluster management.
detail: Container Apps sit between Azure Functions and AKS in the control spectrum. The platform abstracts Kubernetes and KEDA, letting teams focus on container configuration, scaling rules, traffic policies, secrets, managed identity, and observability. Each app runs as one or more replicas inside a shared Container Apps Environment, scales to zero when idle, and routes traffic across revisions for safe deployments. Dapr integration adds distributed application runtime capabilities — state, pub/sub, service invocation, and bindings — as a sidecar. .NET Aspire can target Container Apps for cloud deployment directly from the AppHost manifest.

concepts.title: Container Apps Environment
concepts.description: A shared boundary for a group of container apps that provides a virtual network, internal DNS, log sink, Dapr configuration, and workload profile selection.

concepts.title: Revisions and traffic splitting
concepts.description: Each deployment creates a new immutable revision; traffic can be split across revisions by percentage for canary releases, A/B tests, or safe rollouts.

concepts.title: Scaling rules
concepts.description: Apps scale on HTTP concurrency, CPU, memory, Azure Service Bus queue depth, or custom KEDA scalers — including scale-to-zero for cost efficiency.

concepts.title: Dapr integration
concepts.description: Enabling Dapr adds a sidecar that provides state management, pub/sub messaging, service invocation, secret access, and output bindings without SDK coupling.

architecture.description: External traffic enters through managed ingress, routes to the active revision of a container app inside the environment, which scales with demand and calls dependencies via internal DNS or Dapr.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: A .NET Aspire AppHost publishes the Orders API to Azure Container Apps using the Azure Developer CLI publisher — the same local orchestration model extends to the cloud.

bestPractices: Use a dedicated Container Apps Environment per workload group or environment tier; share an environment only for apps that genuinely need internal DNS resolution between them.
Set minimum replicas to zero for background workers and event-driven apps, but keep at least one replica for APIs where cold-start latency affects user experience.
Prefer managed identity and Azure RBAC for all resource access; store secrets as Container Apps secrets or Key Vault references, never in image layers or environment literals.
Define scaling rules from measured load rather than defaults — HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU rules should match real traffic patterns observed in staging.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Azure Container Apps over AKS?
interviewQuestions.answer: Container Apps suits teams that need container-based deployment, scale-to-zero, HTTP ingress, and event-driven scaling without managing Kubernetes cluster infrastructure, upgrades, node pools, or networking. AKS is the right choice when workloads need Kubernetes APIs, custom operators, specialised node types, cluster-level networking policy, or capabilities that Container Apps does not expose.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Container App revision and a deployment in Kubernetes?
interviewQuestions.answer: A revision is an immutable snapshot of an app's container image, environment, and scale configuration. Revisions are retained and traffic can be split across them by percentage, enabling canary releases without a separate ingress controller or rollout strategy resource.

interviewQuestions.question: What does Dapr add when enabled on a Container App?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dapr injects a sidecar that provides state management, pub/sub messaging, service-to-service invocation, secret access, and output bindings through a consistent local HTTP or gRPC API. Application code calls the sidecar rather than cloud-specific SDKs, reducing coupling to a particular broker or state store.

note: Container Apps abstracts Kubernetes but still runs on it — understanding replica behaviour, cold starts, revision limits, environment quotas, and networking boundaries matters for production design even though the cluster is not directly managed.
tip: Start with the .NET Aspire Azure Container Apps publisher so the same AppHost that describes your local topology generates the cloud deployment manifest — this keeps local and cloud parity without a separate infrastructure definition.
warning: Scale-to-zero means a first request after idle hits a cold start; measure startup time under real configuration and dependencies before committing to zero minimum replicas for latency-sensitive paths.
latestNote: New guide on revisions, scaling, Dapr, and Aspire deployment to Container Apps

name: Azure Well-Architected Framework
shortDescription: Evaluate Azure workload quality across reliability, security, cost, operations, and performance with explicit tradeoffs.
overview: The Azure Well-Architected Framework is a design framework for improving workload quality through five connected pillars of architectural excellence.
detail: The framework helps workload teams reason about Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency from requirements through production learning. Each pillar supplies design principles, checklists, key strategies, tradeoffs, patterns, and a maturity model. The goal is not a perfect score or a one-time review: teams make intentional tradeoffs, record risks, prioritize improvements, and repeat the free Azure Well-Architected Review as the workload and business context evolve.

concepts.title: Five connected pillars
concepts.description: Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency provide distinct lenses on one workload.

concepts.title: Requirements and tradeoffs
concepts.description: Business criticality, compliance, budget, and time-to-market determine priorities; improving one pillar can introduce costs or risks in another.

concepts.title: Review and improve
concepts.description: The Well-Architected Review identifies risks and produces recommendations that teams can prioritize, own, and reassess over time.

concepts.title: Layered guidance
concepts.description: Pillar guidance establishes fundamentals, while workload, service, and design guides apply them to specific architectures and Azure choices.

architecture.description: Business requirements and workload context drive a five-pillar review, which produces prioritized risks and an iterative improvement backlog.

code.label: WorkloadTargets.cs
code.introduction: Architecture discussions become actionable when the team records measurable workload targets before choosing services or patterns.

bestPractices: Define workload boundaries, critical user flows, measurable targets, constraints, and accountable owners before starting the review.
Evaluate all five pillars together and document accepted tradeoffs instead of optimizing one dimension in isolation.
Turn findings into a prioritized backlog with risk, impact, effort, owner, due date, and verification evidence.
Repeat the review after material architecture changes and on a regular cadence; treat the score as a moving indicator, not a compliance badge.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Azure Well-Architected Framework?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is Microsoft guidance for improving Azure workload quality across Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency through principles, checklists, strategies, tradeoffs, patterns, and assessments.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Azure Well-Architected Review and when should you run it?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a free assessment that compares workload design choices with framework recommendations. Run it during design, before major releases, after material changes, and periodically in production.

interviewQuestions.question: Can a workload maximize every pillar at the same time?
interviewQuestions.answer: Usually not. Higher availability, stronger controls, or lower latency can add cost and operational complexity, so teams must make business-aligned tradeoffs and record accepted risks.

note: The framework evaluates a workload, not an entire Azure estate or landing zone. Portfolio governance and platform readiness require complementary guidance such as the Cloud Adoption Framework.
tip: Start with critical flows and the highest business risks, then use the review recommendations to build a small, owned improvement backlog.
warning: Do not treat a Well-Architected score as proof of production readiness; validate recommendations with tests, telemetry, drills, and operational evidence.
latestNote: New foundation guide to the five pillars and Well-Architected Review

name: WAF: Reliability
shortDescription: Design critical flows to withstand faults, recover within business targets, and remain operable under real failure conditions.
overview: The Reliability pillar focuses on resiliency, availability, recovery, and the workload's ability to return to a functioning state after failure.
detail: Reliable design begins with business requirements and critical flows, then translates them into availability targets, recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives, and service-level indicators. Teams use redundancy, fault isolation, retries, timeouts, health models, backups, disaster recovery, and controlled fault testing to meet those targets. Simplicity matters: every resilience mechanism adds state, cost, dependencies, and failure modes that operators must understand.

concepts.title: Targets and critical flows
concepts.description: Availability SLOs, RTO, RPO, and dependency objectives must be derived from business impact for the flows that matter most.

concepts.title: Redundancy and fault isolation
concepts.description: Availability zones, scale units, partitioning, and independent failure domains reduce the blast radius of component or datacenter failures.

concepts.title: Self-healing and recovery
concepts.description: Timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, health endpoints, failover, backups, and tested restore procedures return service safely.

concepts.title: Failure testing
concepts.description: Load tests, chaos experiments, game days, and disaster-recovery drills verify assumptions before an uncontrolled incident does.

architecture.description: Traffic is routed across isolated instances while health signals, resilience policies, and recovery data support detection, failover, and restoration.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: ASP.NET Core health checks and the standard HTTP resilience handler provide observable readiness plus bounded retries, timeouts, and circuit breaking for an outbound dependency.

bestPractices: Set reliability targets per critical flow and include dependency availability in the end-to-end model.
Prefer bounded retries with jitter and idempotent operations; combine them with timeouts and circuit breaking to avoid retry storms.
Use availability zones or regions only when business targets justify the extra cost and operational complexity, and test failover regularly.
Back up data according to RPO, restore according to RTO, and prove both through automated validation and scheduled recovery drills.

interviewQuestions.question: How does designing for 99.9% availability differ from 99.99%?
interviewQuestions.answer: 99.99% allows roughly one tenth of the downtime of 99.9%, often requiring stronger redundancy, faster detection and recovery, fewer maintenance interruptions, stricter dependency targets, more automation, and higher cost.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
interviewQuestions.answer: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after disruption. RPO is the maximum acceptable data-loss window measured backward from the failure.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can retries make an outage worse?
interviewQuestions.answer: Unbounded or synchronized retries multiply traffic against a failing dependency, exhaust resources, and delay recovery. Retries need limits, backoff, jitter, time budgets, and idempotency.

note: An Azure service SLA is an input to workload reliability; it is not the workload's end-to-end SLO.
tip: Build a failure-mode analysis for one critical flow and map every dependency, detection signal, mitigation, and recovery owner.
warning: A backup that has never been restored under realistic conditions is an unverified recovery assumption.
latestNote: New pillar guide on targets, fault isolation, resilience, and recovery

name: WAF: Security
shortDescription: Protect workload confidentiality, integrity, and availability through zero trust, defense in depth, and continuous improvement.
overview: The Security pillar protects data and systems through risk-aware controls for confidentiality, integrity, availability, detection, and response.
detail: Security is a continuous workload discipline rather than a perimeter feature. Teams establish a baseline, classify assets and data, model threats, verify identity explicitly, grant least privilege, segment components, encrypt data, harden resources, protect secrets, monitor suspicious behavior, test controls, and prepare incident response. Azure services such as Microsoft Entra ID, managed identities, Key Vault, Private Link, Azure Policy, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud support the strategy, but the workload team remains accountable for secure application behavior.

concepts.title: Zero Trust identity
concepts.description: Authenticate and authorize every request using explicit identity, least privilege, short-lived credentials, and contextual policy rather than network location alone.

concepts.title: Data protection
concepts.description: Classify data, minimize collection, encrypt in transit and at rest, protect keys, and control where sensitive values can flow.

concepts.title: Threat-driven design
concepts.description: Threat models identify assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, mitigations, and residual risks before implementation choices harden.

concepts.title: Detection and response
concepts.description: Security telemetry, Defender for Cloud, alert triage, playbooks, evidence retention, and exercises reduce time to contain incidents.

architecture.description: Identity-aware edge and application controls protect segmented workload components, while centralized security telemetry supports detection and response.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A fallback authorization policy makes authenticated access the default while a named policy requires an explicit application permission for sensitive endpoints.

bestPractices: Create and maintain a threat model for critical flows, trust boundaries, privileged actions, and third-party integrations.
Use managed identities and workload identity federation, apply least-privilege roles, and eliminate long-lived application credentials where possible.
Encrypt transport and storage, centralize key and secret management, and design rotation and revocation before production.
Integrate secure coding, dependency scanning, configuration policy, penetration testing, security monitoring, and incident exercises into the delivery lifecycle.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Zero Trust change Azure workload design?
interviewQuestions.answer: It removes implicit trust based on network location. Every access is explicitly authenticated, authorized with least privilege, evaluated in context, logged, and assumed potentially hostile.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Azure Policy and Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
interviewQuestions.answer: Azure Policy evaluates and can enforce resource configuration rules. Defender for Cloud combines posture recommendations with workload protection and threat detection; the services complement each other.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is encryption not enough to secure data?
interviewQuestions.answer: Encryption protects specific states and paths, but compromised identities, excessive permissions, application flaws, exposed keys, logs, backups, or decrypted processing can still disclose or alter data.

note: Security controls must preserve workload availability; aggressive blocking without safe recovery paths can create a denial of service.
tip: Use managed identity for every supported Azure-to-Azure connection and review the remaining credential inventory as explicit security debt.
warning: Do not rely on a private network as the authorization boundary; compromised or misconfigured internal callers still require identity and policy checks.
latestNote: New pillar guide on Zero Trust, data protection, and threat response

name: WAF: Cost Optimization
shortDescription: Build financial accountability into architecture with cost models, usage and rate optimization, budgets, and continuous FinOps feedback.
overview: The Cost Optimization pillar sustains workload return on investment by modeling cost, setting guardrails, reducing waste, and optimizing usage and rates.
detail: Cost-efficient architecture connects spending to business value. Teams establish ownership and budgets, model expected demand, allocate costs with tags and subscriptions, measure unit economics, right-size resources, scale with usage, choose appropriate pricing commitments, remove waste, and revisit decisions as demand and Azure pricing change. Cost is balanced with reliability, security, operational effort, and performance rather than minimized in isolation.

concepts.title: Cost model and guardrails
concepts.description: Forecast workload components, environments, data, traffic, support, and growth; then use budgets and alerts to expose variance early.

concepts.title: Usage optimization
concepts.description: Right-sizing, autoscaling, scheduling, storage lifecycle, efficient queries, and removing idle resources align consumption with real demand.

concepts.title: Rate optimization
concepts.description: Reservations, savings plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit, tiers, and negotiated pricing reduce unit rates only when usage is understood.

concepts.title: FinOps feedback
concepts.description: Engineering, finance, and product teams share ownership through allocation, unit metrics, anomaly review, forecasting, and prioritized action.

architecture.description: Tagged workload usage flows into cost allocation and unit metrics, which drive budgets, alerts, forecasts, and architecture optimization decisions.

code.label: UsageMetrics.cs
code.introduction: Low-cardinality business usage metrics let teams compare Azure spend with delivered value instead of looking only at a monthly total.

bestPractices: Assign cost ownership and allocation metadata to every resource, environment, shared service, and data path.
Track business-aligned unit costs such as cost per order or tenant alongside total spend and technical utilization.
Right-size and autoscale from measured demand, then use pricing commitments only for a stable, well-understood baseline.
Review anomalies, idle assets, data growth, egress, license benefits, and forecast variance on a regular engineering and finance cadence.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between usage optimization and rate optimization?
interviewQuestions.answer: Usage optimization reduces or reshapes consumed resources. Rate optimization lowers the price paid for expected consumption through commitments, benefits, or tier choices.

interviewQuestions.question: When can an Azure reservation increase cost?
interviewQuestions.answer: A commitment can waste money when demand falls, workloads move, the chosen scope or SKU is wrong, or teams reserve capacity before establishing a stable baseline.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you balance cost optimization with reliability?
interviewQuestions.answer: Start from business targets and critical flows, quantify the cost and risk of redundancy or recovery options, optimize noncritical paths differently, and record accepted tradeoffs.

note: The cheapest architecture is not necessarily cost-efficient if it misses business outcomes or consumes disproportionate engineering time.
tip: Create one unit-cost dashboard that joins allocated Azure cost with a stable business usage metric and review its trend, not just its current value.
warning: Do not purchase long-term commitments to hide idle capacity; eliminate waste and establish a stable usage baseline first.
latestNote: New pillar guide on cost models, FinOps, usage, and rate optimization

name: WAF: Operational Excellence
shortDescription: Operate and evolve workloads through DevOps culture, standards, automation, observability, and safe deployment practices.
overview: The Operational Excellence pillar uses standardized processes, team cohesion, observability, automation, and safe delivery to sustain workload quality.
detail: Operational excellence connects how a workload is built, released, observed, supported, and improved. Teams define ownership and standards, automate repeatable work, manage infrastructure as code, build a trustworthy supply chain, collect actionable telemetry, deploy progressively, maintain runbooks, learn from incidents, and reduce toil. The objective is not maximum tooling; it is consistent, low-risk change and fast learning across development and operations.

concepts.title: DevOps culture and ownership
concepts.description: Cross-functional teams share responsibility for design, delivery, production health, support, learning, and continuous improvement.

concepts.title: Automation and IaC
concepts.description: Versioned infrastructure, policy, tests, pipelines, and repeatable runbooks reduce drift and manual error while preserving reviewability.

concepts.title: Holistic observability
concepts.description: Correlated logs, metrics, traces, health models, dashboards, and alerts explain user impact and support diagnosis.

concepts.title: Safe deployment
concepts.description: Small changes, deployment rings, health gates, feature flags, rollback or roll-forward plans, and post-deployment observation limit blast radius.

architecture.description: A versioned supply chain promotes tested artifacts and infrastructure through guarded deployment rings while telemetry and incident learning feed improvements back to source.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: OpenTelemetry creates correlated traces and metrics that can be exported to an observability backend and used by deployment health gates.

bestPractices: Keep application and infrastructure definitions versioned, reviewable, reproducible, and promoted from the same tested artifacts.
Define service ownership, health models, actionable alerts, runbooks, escalation paths, and incident roles before production.
Release through progressive rings with automated quality and health gates, an explicit rollback or roll-forward path, and adequate observation time.
Run blameless incident reviews, track corrective actions to completion, and automate recurring operational toil.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes an alert actionable?
interviewQuestions.answer: It represents meaningful user or system impact, has a clear owner and urgency, includes diagnostic context, and links to a tested response or escalation path.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use deployment rings?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rings expose a change to progressively larger and more representative audiences, limiting blast radius while health signals validate the release before wider promotion.

interviewQuestions.question: How is observability different from monitoring?
interviewQuestions.answer: Monitoring checks known conditions. Observability uses rich telemetry and system context to investigate both known and previously unanticipated internal states from external signals.

note: Operational excellence is a property of the sociotechnical system: ownership, incentives, processes, and learning matter as much as tools.
tip: Choose one critical service and verify that an on-call engineer can identify impact, find the owning change, and execute the recovery runbook from its alert.
warning: Automation without safe defaults, approvals, idempotency, auditability, and recovery can accelerate failure instead of improving operations.
latestNote: New pillar guide on DevOps, observability, IaC, and safe delivery

name: WAF: Performance Efficiency
shortDescription: Meet changing workload demand efficiently with measurable targets, suitable services, scaling, partitioning, caching, and testing.
overview: The Performance Efficiency pillar helps workloads meet demand efficiently through realistic targets, scalable design, measurement, testing, and continuous optimization.
detail: Performance efficiency begins with critical flows and measurable latency, throughput, concurrency, and capacity targets. Teams choose services and SKUs that fit access patterns, scale horizontally, partition data and work, cache intentionally, use asynchronous processing, reduce network distance, and validate behavior with production-shaped load tests. Cloud elasticity reduces the need for fixed long-term capacity predictions, but effective autoscaling still needs leading signals, safe limits, warm-up behavior, and cost awareness.

concepts.title: Performance targets
concepts.description: Percentile latency, throughput, concurrency, saturation, and freshness targets should be measurable per critical flow and tied to user outcomes.

concepts.title: Scaling and partitioning
concepts.description: Horizontal scale, stateless compute, partition keys, queues, and independent scale units distribute work while containing hotspots.

concepts.title: Caching and edge delivery
concepts.description: Application caches, distributed caches, output caching, CDNs, and data locality reduce repeated work when freshness and invalidation are explicit.

concepts.title: Testing and optimization
concepts.description: Baseline, load, stress, soak, and failover tests expose bottlenecks; telemetry and profiles guide changes instead of intuition.

architecture.description: Edge caching and load distribution feed horizontally scalable services, which use partitioned data and asynchronous work while telemetry drives autoscaling and optimization.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: HybridCache reduces repeated dependency work and coordinates concurrent cache misses while preserving cancellation and a bounded freshness window.

bestPractices: Define percentile latency, throughput, concurrency, saturation, and capacity targets for critical flows before selecting optimizations.
Load test with realistic data, request mixes, dependency behavior, warm-up, cache state, and failure conditions in an environment representative of production.
Scale on signals that lead user impact, set minimum and maximum capacity, and test scale-out, scale-in, cold start, and hotspot behavior.
Cache only with an explicit key strategy, freshness requirement, invalidation approach, size boundary, miss behavior, and observability.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use p95 or p99 latency instead of only averages?
interviewQuestions.answer: Averages hide slow-tail experiences. Percentiles show the latency threshold experienced by most users and expose outliers that often indicate saturation, retries, or uneven partitions.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a good autoscaling signal?
interviewQuestions.answer: It correlates with demand or impending saturation, arrives early enough to add capacity, avoids excessive noise, and is paired with tested limits, cooldowns, and failure behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How can caching harm performance or correctness?
interviewQuestions.answer: Poor keys, stale data, unbounded memory, synchronized expiry, cache stampedes, expensive serialization, and dependency failure on misses can increase latency or return incorrect results.

note: Performance efficiency is not maximum speed at any cost; it is meeting workload targets with proportionate resources and sustainable operations.
tip: Establish a production-shaped baseline before optimization, then change one bottleneck at a time and compare the same percentiles and resource signals.
warning: Autoscaling cannot compensate for a hard database bottleneck, hot partition, serialized critical section, or dependency quota.
latestNote: New pillar guide on targets, scaling, caching, partitioning, and load testing

name: GraphQL in .NET
shortDescription: Build flexible, schema-first APIs in .NET using Hot Chocolate — letting clients query exactly the data they need with strong typing, resolvers, and subscriptions.
overview: GraphQL is a query language for APIs that lets clients specify exactly which fields they need, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching in a single typed contract.
detail: Hot Chocolate is the leading .NET GraphQL server library. It generates a strongly typed schema from C# types using code-first or annotation-based approaches, handles query parsing, validation, and execution, and integrates with ASP.NET Core middleware, dependency injection, Entity Framework Core, and OpenTelemetry. Clients send a POST request with a query document and receive exactly the shape they asked for — no more, no less. Mutations change state; subscriptions stream real-time updates over WebSockets. The DataLoader pattern batches and deduplicates database calls within a single request to avoid the N+1 query problem.

concepts.title: Schema, types, and resolvers
concepts.description: The schema defines every type, field, query, mutation, and subscription the API exposes. A resolver is the function that fetches or computes the value for one field — analogous to a controller action but composable and field-scoped.

concepts.title: Queries, mutations, and subscriptions
concepts.description: Queries read data; mutations write data and return the updated state; subscriptions open a WebSocket connection and push updates when server-side state changes — all described in the same schema.

concepts.title: DataLoader and the N+1 problem
concepts.description: A DataLoader batches individual field-level resolver calls into a single bulk database query per request cycle, preventing the N+1 problem that occurs when each item in a list triggers a separate query.

concepts.title: Persisted queries
concepts.description: Clients register query documents at build time and send only a hash at runtime. The server executes only pre-approved queries, reducing payload size, preventing arbitrary query attacks, and enabling query-level caching.

architecture.description: The client sends a typed query document; Hot Chocolate validates it against the schema, resolves each field using injected services or DataLoaders, and returns a single JSON response shaped to the query.

code.label: OrderQuery.cs
code.introduction: A code-first query type exposes orders with a DataLoader to batch product lookups — the client gets exactly the fields it asks for and the server makes one product query regardless of how many order lines are returned.

bestPractices: Always set query depth and complexity limits — an unbounded GraphQL query can trigger exponential resolver execution and take down a server. Hot Chocolate provides MaxExecutionDepth and cost analysis middleware.
Use DataLoaders for any resolver that loads a related entity by ID — without them, a list of 50 orders with product details triggers 50 separate database calls in a single request.
Use persisted queries in production to prevent arbitrary query execution, reduce payload size, and enable query-level response caching at the CDN or gateway layer.

Expose GraphQL alongside REST rather than as a replacement — REST suits simple CRUD and public third-party APIs; GraphQL suits complex client-driven queries, BFF aggregation, and mobile clients with bandwidth constraints.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does GraphQL solve that REST does not handle well?
interviewQuestions.answer: REST endpoints return fixed shapes — clients either get too much data for their needs or must call multiple endpoints and assemble the result. GraphQL lets the client declare exactly which fields it needs in a single request, eliminating over-fetching, under-fetching, and the waterfall of requests common in REST-based mobile applications.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how does DataLoader solve it?
interviewQuestions.answer: When resolving a list of items, each item's child fields are resolved individually — a list of 100 orders each triggering a separate product query results in 101 database calls. DataLoader collects all product ID requests made during one execution cycle, issues a single bulk query for all of them, and distributes the results back to each resolver — reducing 101 calls to 2.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose GraphQL over REST for a .NET API?
interviewQuestions.answer: GraphQL is a strong fit when multiple clients need different shapes of the same data — a web app, a mobile app, and a BFF — when query flexibility matters more than cache simplicity, or when aggregating data from several services in a single request. REST remains better for simple CRUD resources, public APIs with broad tooling expectations, HTTP caching requirements, and teams less familiar with GraphQL's operational complexity.

note: GraphQL shifts query complexity from the server to the schema design — a poorly designed schema with overly connected types becomes hard to secure, version, and optimise; treat schema design with the same care as REST API design.
tip: Start with Hot Chocolate's annotation-based approach and UseProjection, UseFiltering, and UseSorting attributes on EF Core queryable resolvers — this gives clients flexible querying with database-level filtering before writing a single custom resolver.
warning: GraphQL introspection exposes the full schema to any client — disable or restrict it in production environments to avoid leaking internal type names, field names, and relationships to external callers.
latestNote: New guide on schema-first design, resolvers, DataLoader, and persisted queries with Hot Chocolate

name: Webhook Patterns
shortDescription: Receive, validate, process, and reliably handle inbound HTTP callbacks from third-party platforms with signature verification and idempotent consumers.
overview: Webhooks are HTTP callbacks a third-party platform sends to your endpoint when something happens on their side. Receiving them reliably requires signature verification, fast acknowledgement, idempotent processing, and a durable handoff to background work.
detail: Payment providers, source control platforms, and SaaS products push events to a URL you register rather than waiting for you to poll. The receiving endpoint must verify the request is genuine using an HMAC signature, return a 200 immediately to prevent the sender retrying, and hand the payload to a background processor that handles business logic durably. Because senders retry on failure or timeout, every handler must be idempotent. The same webhook event may arrive multiple times, out of order, or after a significant delay.

concepts.title: Signature verification
concepts.description: The sender includes an HMAC signature computed from the raw request body and a shared secret. The receiver recomputes the signature and rejects the request if it does not match, preventing spoofed events.

concepts.title: Immediate acknowledgement
concepts.description: Return HTTP 200 within seconds of receiving the webhook — most platforms retry if they do not get a quick response. Business logic runs asynchronously after the acknowledgement, not inside the receiving request.

concepts.title: Idempotent processing
concepts.description: The same webhook event may be delivered more than once. The processor records processed event identifiers and skips re-execution when a duplicate arrives, preventing double charges, double emails, or duplicate records.

concepts.title: Durable handoff
concepts.description: The receiving endpoint writes the raw payload to a durable store — a database outbox or a queue — before responding. A background worker processes it, decoupling reception from business logic and surviving restarts.

architecture.description: The inbound webhook endpoint verifies the signature, writes the raw payload to an outbox, returns 200, and a background worker processes the event idempotently from the outbox.

code.label: WebhookEndpoint.cs
code.introduction: The endpoint reads the raw body before model binding, verifies the HMAC signature using the shared secret, stores the payload durably, and returns 200 — all before any business logic runs.

bestPractices: Always use a constant-time comparison such as CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals when comparing HMAC signatures — standard string equality is vulnerable to timing attacks.
Read and verify the raw request body before any model binding or middleware transforms it; some frameworks buffer or modify the body stream, which invalidates the signature.
Persist the raw payload to an inbox or outbox table before returning 200, so a crash between acknowledgement and processing does not silently drop the event.
Design webhook processors as idempotent consumers and record the platform's event identifier in the same transaction as the business effect, so duplicate delivery is safe to retry.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should business logic not run inside the webhook receiving endpoint?
interviewQuestions.answer: Most platforms have a short response timeout — often five to thirty seconds — after which they mark the delivery as failed and retry. Business logic involving database writes, external calls, or message publishing can easily exceed that window. Acknowledging immediately and handing off to a background processor decouples reception from processing and prevents unnecessary retries.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a timing attack and why does it matter for HMAC verification?
interviewQuestions.answer: A timing attack measures how long a comparison takes to infer whether the guess is partially correct. Standard string equality returns early on the first mismatch, leaking information through response time variance. CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals always takes the same time regardless of where strings differ, making the comparison safe.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle webhook events that arrive out of order?
interviewQuestions.answer: Most webhook events carry a timestamp and event type. The processor should check whether the event represents a state that the current aggregate state can transition to. If an older event arrives after a newer one has already been applied, the processor can detect and skip it using the recorded event sequence or a status field on the aggregate.

note: Webhook reliability depends on the sender's retry policy, not yours — design the receiver to be tolerant of duplicates, delays, and reordering from day one rather than treating these as edge cases.
tip: Register a dedicated webhook endpoint per platform rather than a single generic one — it simplifies routing, secret management, signature scheme differences, and per-provider monitoring and alerting.
warning: Never trust the event payload alone to authorise a business action — a verified signature proves the request came from the platform, but the payload content should still be validated against your own database state before processing.
latestNote: New guide on signature verification, immediate acknowledgement, idempotent processing, and durable handoff

name: Backend for Frontend
shortDescription: Give each frontend its own tailored API layer instead of forcing every client through one general-purpose API.
overview: A Backend for Frontend is a thin API layer built and owned for one specific client—web, mobile, or a partner integration—that aggregates and reshapes calls to backend services into exactly what that client needs.
detail: Instead of one general-purpose API serving every client's differing needs with optional fields and version branches, each frontend gets its own BFF: composing multiple backend calls into one response, hiding backend topology, and evolving independently of other clients' needs. The tradeoff is more services to own and keep consistent, so BFFs work best when client needs have genuinely diverged, not as a default for every project.

concepts.title: Client-owned aggregation
concepts.description: A BFF composes calls to multiple backend services into the single shaped response its one client actually needs.

concepts.title: Reduced client-side complexity
concepts.description: Moving aggregation, retries, and field shaping into the BFF keeps client code focused on presentation instead of backend orchestration.

concepts.title: Independent evolution
concepts.description: Each BFF can change its contract and pace of release without coordinating with unrelated frontends sharing the same backend.

concepts.title: Backend topology hiding
concepts.description: Clients depend on their BFF's contract, not on the internal service boundaries behind it, so backend services can be refactored without breaking clients.

architecture.description: A frontend calls its own BFF, which aggregates and reshapes calls to shared backend services into that client's specific response shape.

code.label: WebBffEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: A BFF endpoint composes two backend calls into the single shape the web client actually renders.

bestPractices: Create a new BFF only once a client's needs have genuinely diverged from others, not preemptively for every frontend.
Keep a BFF thin—composition and shaping, not business logic that belongs in the backend services it calls.
Own each BFF with the team that owns its frontend, so contract changes don't require cross-team coordination.
Apply the same resilience patterns—timeouts, retries, circuit breakers—to a BFF's outbound calls as any other service-to-service call.

interviewQuestions.question: How is a BFF different from an API gateway?
interviewQuestions.answer: A gateway is typically one shared entry point applying cross-cutting concerns like routing, auth, and rate limiting for many clients; a BFF is dedicated to one client, aggregating and shaping backend calls into that client's specific needs—the two are often used together, gateway in front of multiple BFFs.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a BFF solve that a single shared API doesn't?
interviewQuestions.answer: A shared API serving very different clients accumulates optional fields, version branches, and client-specific logic to satisfy everyone; a BFF lets each client's API evolve and be shaped independently, avoiding that shared complexity.

interviewQuestions.question: What's the main cost of adopting the BFF pattern?
interviewQuestions.answer: More services to build, deploy, and keep consistent—logic like authorization or validation can end up duplicated across BFFs unless it's deliberately kept in shared backend services instead.

note: A BFF is scoped to one client's needs, not a second general-purpose API sitting in front of your services.
tip: Let the frontend team that owns the client also own its BFF; the pattern's main value is removing cross-team coordination from client-specific changes.
warning: Duplicating business rules—not just response shaping—across multiple BFFs recreates the consistency problems the pattern was meant to avoid.
latestNote: New guide on client-owned API aggregation

name: Terraform
shortDescription: Declare cloud infrastructure as versioned, reviewable code that can be planned before it's applied, across any provider.
overview: Terraform describes infrastructure—networks, databases, compute, permissions—as declarative configuration, then plans and applies the changes needed to make real infrastructure match that configuration.
detail: A provider maps Terraform's HCL configuration to a specific cloud's APIs, so the same workflow applies whether you're targeting Azure, AWS, or another platform. Terraform tracks real infrastructure in a state file, computes a plan showing exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed before anything happens, and lets teams share reusable modules for common infrastructure shapes.

concepts.title: Providers
concepts.description: A provider translates Terraform configuration into calls against a specific platform's API, letting one tool and workflow target multiple clouds.

concepts.title: State
concepts.description: Terraform records the real infrastructure it manages in a state file, using it to compute the difference between desired and actual on every run.

concepts.title: Plan and apply
concepts.description: Plan shows exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed before anything happens; apply executes only that reviewed plan.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.description: Reusable, parameterized configuration packages let teams share a tested infrastructure shape—like a standard app environment—instead of duplicating raw resources.

architecture.description: Configuration is planned against current state to compute a diff, then applied through the provider to create the real infrastructure.

code.label: main.tf
code.introduction: A module call provisions a standard app environment with parameters instead of duplicating the underlying resources per project.

bestPractices: Store state remotely with locking so two runs can't apply conflicting changes to the same infrastructure at once.
Always review a plan's output before applying it, especially destroy actions—treat plan as a required gate, not a formality.
Package repeated infrastructure shapes as modules with clear inputs and outputs instead of copy-pasting resource blocks.
Keep secrets out of state and configuration; reference them from a secrets manager instead of hardcoding values.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Terraform state, and why does losing it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: State is Terraform's record of the real infrastructure it manages, used to compute what's changed on every run; without it, Terraform has no way to know what already exists and can plan to recreate or orphan real resources.

interviewQuestions.question: Why review a Terraform plan before applying it?
interviewQuestions.answer: The plan shows exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed as a result of a configuration change, catching unintended consequences—like a destroy triggered by a renamed resource—before they happen against real infrastructure.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem do Terraform modules solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: They let a team package a tested, parameterized shape of infrastructure—like a standard app environment—and reuse it across projects, instead of every project hand-writing and maintaining its own copy of similar resource blocks.

note: Terraform's plan/apply split exists specifically so infrastructure changes can be reviewed like code changes, before they touch anything real.
tip: Run Terraform in CI with a required plan-review step on every pull request, the same way you'd require a code review.
warning: Manually changing infrastructure that Terraform manages, outside of Terraform, causes state drift that can lead to a later apply silently reverting or fighting your manual change.
latestNote: New guide on providers, state, and plan/apply

name: Secrets Management
shortDescription: Keep credentials, keys, and connection strings out of source and configuration, with rotation and least-privilege access built in.
overview: Secrets management is about where credentials live, who and what can read them, and how they get replaced—not just picking a vault product to store them in.
detail: A secret checked into source control or left in a plain configuration file is a secret that's already leaked, because history, backups, and logs outlive any later attempt to remove it. A dedicated secrets store centralizes access control and auditing, workload identity removes the need for an application to hold its own long-lived credential to reach that store, and rotation limits how long a compromised secret stays useful.

concepts.title: Centralized storage and access control
concepts.description: A dedicated secrets store lets access be granted, audited, and revoked per identity, instead of secrets being copied into every environment's configuration.

concepts.title: Workload identity
concepts.description: Letting a compute resource authenticate to the secrets store using its platform identity removes the need for a bootstrap credential to fetch other credentials.

concepts.title: Rotation
concepts.description: Regularly replacing secrets, ideally automatically, limits how long a leaked or compromised credential remains valid.

concepts.title: Least privilege scoping
concepts.description: An application or service should only be able to read the specific secrets it needs, not every secret in a shared vault.

architecture.description: A workload authenticates with its platform identity, requests only the secrets it needs from the vault, and the vault logs and can later rotate that access.

code.label: SecretsSetup.cs
code.introduction: The application authenticates to the vault using its managed identity, with no credential stored in configuration to reach it.

bestPractices: Never commit a secret to source control, even temporarily—rotate it immediately if it happens, since history retains it.
Use a workload's platform identity to authenticate to the vault instead of storing a separate credential to reach the vault itself.
Scope access policies per secret or per group of secrets, not one broad policy granting every workload read access to everything.
Automate rotation for anything long-lived, and design applications to pick up a rotated secret without a manual restart.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is committing a secret to source control dangerous even if you delete it in the next commit?
interviewQuestions.answer: Git history retains every prior version by default, and the secret may already be in forks, backups, CI logs, or cached clones, so deleting it from the latest commit doesn't remove it from anywhere it's already been.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does workload identity solve for secrets management?
interviewQuestions.answer: Without it, an application needs some credential to authenticate to the secrets store in the first place, which just relocates the original problem; workload identity lets the platform vouch for the application's identity directly, removing that bootstrap credential entirely.

interviewQuestions.question: Why rotate secrets that haven't been confirmed as leaked?
interviewQuestions.answer: You can't always know a secret has leaked—rotation limits the value and window of a leak you don't yet know about, the same way changing a lock periodically doesn't require proof a key was copied.

note: Secrets management is as much about identity and access design as it is about which product stores the values.
tip: Design for rotation from day one—retrofitting a rotation-tolerant application after every secret is hardcoded at startup is much harder than building it in from the start.
warning: A single shared master credential granting broad access to a whole vault defeats much of the purpose of centralizing secrets in the first place.
latestNote: New guide on rotation, workload identity, and least privilege

name: Infrastructure as Code (Bicep)
shortDescription: Define, version, and deploy Azure infrastructure declaratively using Bicep modules, parameter files, deployment stacks, and CI/CD pipelines.
overview: Bicep is Microsoft's domain-specific language for declaring Azure infrastructure as code — compiled to ARM templates, reviewed like application code, and deployed repeatably across environments.
detail: Bicep replaces raw ARM JSON with a clean declarative syntax, strong typing, native module support, and first-class IDE tooling. Infrastructure defined in Bicep is committed to source control, reviewed in pull requests, promoted through environments with parameter files, and deployed by CI/CD pipelines using the Azure CLI or Azure Developer CLI. Deployment stacks extend this model by tracking which resources a deployment owns and cleaning up orphaned resources when the stack is updated or deleted. For .NET teams, Bicep pairs naturally with the azd CLI that Aspire uses for cloud deployments.

concepts.title: Declarative resource definitions
concepts.description: A Bicep file describes the desired state of Azure resources — their type, SKU, location, properties, and dependencies. The platform reconciles current state to match the declaration on each deployment.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.description: A module is a reusable Bicep file that accepts parameters and encapsulates one cohesive set of resources — a module for a Container App, a module for a Key Vault, a module for a SQL server — composable into larger deployments.

concepts.title: Parameter files and environments
concepts.description: Bicepparam files supply environment-specific values — SKUs, capacities, feature flags, connection strings — keeping the template logic environment-neutral and the differences version-controlled and reviewable.

concepts.title: Deployment stacks
concepts.description: A deployment stack tracks all resources deployed as a unit and applies a deny-assignment to prevent out-of-band changes. Updating or deleting the stack reconciles or removes managed resources automatically.

architecture.description: Bicep source is compiled and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline, promoting one validated template with environment-specific parameters from dev through staging to production.

code.label: container-app.bicep
code.introduction: A focused Bicep module deploys a Container App with managed identity, Key Vault secret reference, and environment-linked configuration — accepting only the values that change per environment.

bestPractices: Treat Bicep files as production code — review them in pull requests, lint with the Bicep linter, and enforce no-hardcoded-secrets and explicit API versions as CI checks.
Use modules to encapsulate cohesive resource groups — a Container App module, a networking module — and compose them in a main.bicep rather than putting everything in one large file.
Separate environment-specific values into Bicepparam files and keep template logic environment-neutral so the same compiled template is promoted from dev to prod without modification.
Run what-if deployments in CI before applying to staging or production so reviewers can see exactly which resource properties will change before approving the pipeline run.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an ARM template and a Bicep file?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Bicep file is a higher-level declarative language that compiles to an ARM JSON template. Bicep provides cleaner syntax, type safety, native modules, string interpolation, conditional expressions, and IDE tooling, while ARM JSON is verbose and error-prone to write by hand. The compiled output is identical — Bicep is a transparent abstraction over ARM.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a Bicep deployment stack and when would you use it?
interviewQuestions.answer: A deployment stack tracks all resources deployed as a unit and can apply deny-assignments to prevent out-of-band changes to managed resources. When the stack is updated, resources removed from the template can be detached, deleted, or left in place according to the configured cleanup policy. It is useful when you want the infrastructure definition to be the authoritative source and prevent drift from manual portal changes.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you pass secrets into a Bicep deployment without hardcoding them?
interviewQuestions.answer: Reference secrets from Azure Key Vault using a Bicepparam file with a getSecret() call — this injects the secret value at deployment time from Key Vault without it appearing in source control, pipeline logs, or the compiled template. The deployment identity needs Key Vault Secrets User access on the vault.

note: Bicep defines desired infrastructure state — it does not replace application configuration, secrets management, identity assignment, or monitoring setup, all of which need their own deliberate design.
tip: Start with the Azure Developer CLI and let azd init scaffold the initial Bicep structure for your project — it produces working modules for common patterns like Container Apps with managed identity and Key Vault that you can extend rather than writing from scratch.
warning: A what-if result showing no changes does not guarantee the deployment will succeed — resource provider API changes, quota limits, policy denials, and dependency ordering can still cause failures at apply time.
latestNote: New guide on Bicep modules, parameter files, deployment stacks, and CI/CD promotion

name: Health Checks
shortDescription: Expose meaningful liveness, readiness, and startup signals from .NET applications so orchestrators, load balancers, and dashboards can act on real dependency health.
overview: Health checks expose signals that tell orchestrators, load balancers, and monitoring systems whether an application is alive, ready to serve traffic, and has access to its dependencies.
detail: ASP.NET Core's built-in health check infrastructure lets teams register custom IHealthCheck implementations, group them by tag, filter them per endpoint, and expose results as JSON. Three distinct signals serve different consumers: liveness tells Kubernetes whether to restart the container, readiness tells the load balancer whether to route traffic, and startup tells the orchestrator to wait before applying either probe. Community libraries extend this with pre-built checks for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, URLs, and disk space. The HealthChecks UI library adds a visual dashboard that polls configured endpoints and displays history.

concepts.title: Liveness vs readiness vs startup
concepts.description: Liveness answers 'is the process still functioning?' — failure triggers a container restart. Readiness answers 'is the app ready to serve traffic?' — failure removes the pod from load-balancer rotation. Startup answers 'has initialisation completed?' — used to give slow-starting apps time before liveness kicks in.

concepts.title: Custom IHealthCheck
concepts.description: Any dependency or business invariant can be checked by implementing IHealthCheck and returning Healthy, Degraded, or Unhealthy with a description and optional data dictionary for diagnostic detail.

concepts.title: Tagging and filtering
concepts.description: Health checks are tagged at registration and endpoints use a predicate to select which checks to run — database checks on the readiness endpoint, a trivial always-healthy check on the liveness endpoint.

concepts.title: Health check UI
concepts.description: The AspNetCore.HealthChecks.UI package polls one or more health endpoints on a schedule and renders a dashboard showing current status, history, and failure details — useful for internal operations teams without a full APM tool.

architecture.description: Kubernetes probes call dedicated health endpoints filtered by tag; the readiness endpoint checks real dependencies while the liveness endpoint stays lightweight, and the UI dashboard polls all endpoints for operator visibility.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: Checks are registered with tags, exposed on separate endpoints filtered by tag, and a custom database check demonstrates how to surface a real dependency result with diagnostic data.

bestPractices: Never put real dependency checks on the liveness endpoint — a database outage would restart every healthy pod simultaneously, compounding the incident instead of reducing traffic to the affected node.
Return Degraded rather than Unhealthy for non-critical dependencies such as a cache or secondary queue so the pod stays in rotation but the degraded state is visible to operators and alerts.

Include diagnostic data — active message count, last successful query time, connection pool state — in the health check result so on-call engineers can triage from the health endpoint without needing a separate dashboard.
Set Kubernetes startup probes with a generous failure threshold for apps that run migrations or warm caches on startup; this prevents liveness from restarting a healthy but slow-starting container.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is it dangerous to check database connectivity on the liveness probe?
interviewQuestions.answer: Liveness failure causes Kubernetes to restart the container. If the database goes down, every pod fails liveness simultaneously and Kubernetes restarts them all in a loop — making the outage worse and losing in-flight requests. Liveness should only verify the process itself is alive and not deadlocked. Dependency health belongs on the readiness probe, which removes the pod from traffic rotation without restarting it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Unhealthy and Degraded?
interviewQuestions.answer: Unhealthy means the check has failed and the dependency is not usable — Kubernetes treats it as a readiness failure and stops routing traffic. Degraded means the dependency is reachable but operating below normal — it signals a warning state to monitoring tools while keeping the pod in rotation, allowing operations to investigate without triggering a traffic disruption.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you expose health checks in a microservices system so a central dashboard can monitor all services?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each service exposes a standard JSON health endpoint. A Health Checks UI instance is configured with the URLs of all service endpoints and polls them on a schedule, aggregating status and history in a single dashboard. Alternatively, a monitoring platform such as Azure Monitor or Prometheus scrapes the endpoints and feeds a centralised alerting and visualisation layer.

note: A health check that always returns Healthy is worse than no health check — it builds false confidence. Check the actual dependency, return meaningful status, and include data that helps an on-call engineer act without additional investigation.
tip: Add a dead-letter message count check to your Service Bus or RabbitMQ health check — a rising dead-letter count is one of the earliest signals of a processing problem and is nearly free to surface from the broker's management API.
warning: Health check endpoints should never require authentication from the orchestrator — Kubernetes and load balancers call them without credentials — but restrict them from the public internet using network policy or path-based ingress rules.
latestNote: New guide on liveness, readiness, startup probes, custom checks, and Health Checks UI

name: Orleans
shortDescription: Model distributed state and behavior as virtual actors that the runtime activates, places, and recovers automatically.
overview: Orleans lets you write distributed systems as single-threaded objects called grains, while the runtime handles where each grain runs, how it's activated on demand, and how it recovers after a failure.
detail: A grain is addressed by a stable identity, not a physical location; Orleans activates it on some silo when a call arrives, deactivates it when idle, and reactivates it elsewhere if that silo fails—all transparent to the caller. Because each grain processes messages one at a time, application code inside it can be written without locks, while Orleans handles distribution, placement, and failure recovery underneath.

concepts.title: Grains
concepts.description: A grain is a single-threaded, addressable unit of distributed state and behavior, identified by a stable key rather than a physical location.

concepts.title: Virtual actors
concepts.description: Grains always logically exist; the runtime activates them on demand and deactivates them when idle, so callers never manage a grain's lifecycle directly.

concepts.title: Silos and placement
concepts.description: A cluster of silos hosts grains; Orleans decides where to activate each grain and can reactivate it elsewhere automatically if a silo fails.

concepts.title: Single-threaded execution
concepts.description: Each grain processes one message at a time, so application code inside it avoids the locks and race conditions typical of shared-state concurrency.

architecture.description: A client calls a grain by its identity; the runtime activates it on an available silo, and that grain processes messages one at a time, persisting state as needed.

code.label: OrderGrain.cs
code.introduction: A grain interface and implementation define addressable, single-threaded state; Orleans handles activation and placement.

bestPractices: Keep grain calls single-purpose and short-lived; a grain is a unit of state and behavior, not a place for long synchronous blocking work.
Persist only the state a grain actually needs to recover, and choose a storage provider that matches your durability requirements.
Design grain identities deliberately—they determine how work and state are partitioned across the cluster.
Avoid grain-to-grain call chains that form cycles; they can deadlock since each grain processes one message at a time.

interviewQuestions.question: What does 'virtual actor' mean in Orleans, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: A grain logically always exists at its identity, whether or not it's currently activated in memory; callers never create or destroy it explicitly, and the runtime transparently activates, deactivates, and relocates it, which removes a whole class of lifecycle and placement code the application would otherwise have to write.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Orleans avoid the need for locks inside a grain?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each grain processes incoming calls one at a time, single-threaded, so there's never concurrent access to a grain's own state from within—concurrency exists between grains, not within one.

interviewQuestions.question: What happens to a grain's in-memory state if the silo hosting it fails?
interviewQuestions.answer: The in-memory activation is lost, but if the grain persists its state through a storage provider, Orleans can reactivate it—with that persisted state restored—on another silo when the next call arrives.

note: Orleans trades explicit distributed-systems plumbing for a programming model where distribution is mostly the runtime's problem, not the application's.
tip: Start by modeling your domain's natural single-owner entities—one order, one device, one session—as grains; that mapping is usually where Orleans fits most naturally.
warning: A grain is not a substitute for a database; treat its persisted state as what that one entity needs to recover, not as your system's queryable source of truth.
latestNote: New guide on grains, silos, and virtual actor placement

name: Event Sourcing
shortDescription: Store state as an immutable sequence of domain events and derive current state by replaying them.
overview: Event Sourcing persists the history of what happened to a domain object rather than just its current state, making every change first-class and queryable.
detail: Instead of storing the current row in a database table, an event-sourced system appends a new immutable event every time something meaningful happens to an aggregate. Current state is derived by replaying those events in order. This gives a complete audit trail for free, enables temporal queries, supports event replay into new projections, and makes debugging production incidents far easier. The trade-offs are query complexity, event versioning discipline, and the need for snapshot strategies when event streams grow long.

concepts.title: Event store
concepts.description: An append-only log that persists domain events for each aggregate stream. Events are never updated or deleted — only new events are written.

concepts.title: Aggregate reconstitution
concepts.description: An aggregate is loaded by reading its event stream and applying each event in order, rebuilding current state from history rather than from a snapshot column.

concepts.title: Projections and read models
concepts.description: Read models are built by subscribing to the event stream and projecting events into query-optimised shapes — separate from the write model and rebuildable at any time.

concepts.title: Snapshots
concepts.description: When an aggregate stream grows long, a snapshot captures state at a checkpoint so reconstitution loads the snapshot plus only the events after it.

architecture.description: Commands produce domain events appended to an event store; projections subscribe to the store and populate read models that queries use.

code.label: Order.cs
code.introduction: The aggregate applies events to change its own state; the command handler appends those events to the store rather than saving a mutated entity.

bestPractices: Name events in past tense after meaningful business facts — OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed — not technical operations like OrderUpdated.
Treat event schemas as public contracts; use upcasting or versioned event types to handle schema evolution without rewriting history.
Introduce snapshots only when reconstitution is measurably slow — start without them and add them at a measured stream length threshold.
Keep projections idempotent and rebuildable so a new read model can be populated by replaying the full event history at any time.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the key difference between event sourcing and storing domain events alongside a state record?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event sourcing makes the event stream the source of truth — there is no separate state column to keep in sync. Current state is always derived by replaying events. Storing events alongside a state record is an audit log, not event sourcing, because the state record can diverge from the events.

interviewQuestions.question: How does event sourcing relate to CQRS?
interviewQuestions.answer: They are complementary but independent. CQRS separates read and write models; event sourcing is a write-side persistence strategy. Together, the event store is the authoritative write side and projections populate the read side, but you can use either pattern without the other.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main challenge of event versioning and how do you handle it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Events are immutable, so when a schema needs to change, old events in the store still use the old shape. Upcasting transforms old events to the current schema during loading so the aggregate always sees a consistent version, without rewriting the store.

note: Event sourcing solves the audit and temporal query problem well, but adds complexity around versioning, projection rebuilds, and eventually consistent reads — apply it where that trade-off is genuinely worth making.
tip: Use Marten with PostgreSQL as an event store for a pragmatic .NET start — it gives you append-only streams, snapshots, projections, and async subscriptions without running a separate event store infrastructure.
warning: Do not use event sourcing as a default persistence strategy for every aggregate; apply it where auditability, temporal queries, or event replay provide concrete business value that justifies the operational cost.

name: Redis & Distributed Caching
shortDescription: Speed up .NET applications and reduce database load with Redis for distributed caching, pub/sub, rate limiting, and distributed locks.
overview: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used in .NET applications for distributed caching, session storage, pub/sub messaging, rate limiting, and distributed coordination.
detail: A single-node in-memory cache does not survive restarts and is invisible to other application instances behind a load balancer. Redis solves both problems with a shared, persistent, replicated store. StackExchange.Redis is the standard .NET client; ASP.NET Core integrates Redis through IDistributedCache and output caching middleware. Azure Cache for Redis is the managed option with built-in geo-replication, clustering, and Microsoft Entra authentication. The same Redis instance can serve as a cache, a SignalR backplane, a rate-limit counter store, and a distributed lock provider.

concepts.title: Cache-aside pattern
concepts.description: The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads from the source of truth, populates the cache with a TTL, and returns the value. Eviction and expiry keep the cache from growing unbounded.

concepts.title: IDistributedCache and output caching
concepts.description: IDistributedCache is the ASP.NET Core abstraction for distributed string or byte caches. Output caching middleware caches full HTTP responses at the framework level with Redis as the backing store.

concepts.title: Pub/sub and streams
concepts.description: Redis pub/sub broadcasts messages to all subscribers on a channel, powering SignalR backplanes and lightweight event fan-out. Redis Streams provide a durable, consumer-group-aware alternative.

concepts.title: Distributed locks and rate limiting
concepts.description: The Redlock algorithm uses atomic SET NX EX commands to acquire time-bounded locks across processes. Sliding window and token bucket counters built on INCR and EXPIRE enable per-key rate limiting without a dedicated service.

architecture.description: Application instances share one Redis cluster; cache hits return data without touching the database, while pub/sub channels and lock keys coordinate distributed behaviour across all nodes.

code.label: ProductCache.cs
code.introduction: A typed cache service wraps IDistributedCache with JSON serialisation, a configurable TTL, and safe cache-aside logic — the database is only called on a miss.

bestPractices: Always set an absolute TTL on cached entries; an entry without expiry is a memory leak and a staleness risk as the source of truth evolves.
Use structured, collision-safe key names — prefix by domain and identifier such as product:{id} or session:{userId} — and document the naming convention alongside the cache registration.
Invalidate or update the cache entry in the same operation that mutates the source of truth; invalidating after a separate call risks serving stale data if the second step fails.

Design application code to degrade gracefully when Redis is unavailable — catch connection exceptions, log them, and fall through to the database rather than surfacing a cache infrastructure failure to users.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the cache stampede problem and how do you prevent it?
interviewQuestions.answer: A stampede happens when many requests simultaneously find a cache miss for the same key and all race to load from the database at once, multiplying load. Prevention strategies include probabilistic early expiry, a short-lived Redis lock so only one request rebuilds the entry while others wait or serve the slightly stale value, or background refresh before expiry.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you use Redis pub/sub versus Service Bus or Event Grid?
interviewQuestions.answer: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget with no durability — if a subscriber is offline it misses messages. It suits low-latency fan-out within a trusted environment, such as a SignalR backplane or cache invalidation broadcast. Service Bus and Event Grid provide delivery guarantees, dead-lettering, and durable storage, which are essential for business-critical events.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between IDistributedCache and IMemoryCache in ASP.NET Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: IMemoryCache is in-process, fast, and invisible to other application instances — suitable for single-server or read-heavy non-critical data. IDistributedCache abstracts a shared external store such as Redis, so all instances behind a load balancer share the same data and eviction, at the cost of network latency per cache operation.

note: Redis improves read performance and reduces database load, but it introduces a distributed dependency, consistency trade-offs, memory limits, and connection overhead that must be designed for explicitly.
tip: Use .NET Aspire's AddRedis resource in the AppHost for local development so every developer gets a consistent Redis container without manual setup, and switch to Azure Cache for Redis in production through the same Aspire integration.
warning: Never cache sensitive personal data or security tokens without encryption, short TTLs, and careful key scoping — a cache key collision or overly broad invalidation can expose one user's data to another.
