name: YARP — Reverse Proxy
shortDescription: Build a programmable .NET reverse proxy and API gateway using YARP with route-based forwarding, transforms, load balancing, and middleware integration.
overview: YARP (Yet Another Reverse Proxy) is a Microsoft library for building high-performance, programmable reverse proxies and API gateways directly in .NET using ASP.NET Core middleware.
detail: Unlike infrastructure proxies such as NGINX or managed services such as Azure API Management, YARP runs inside a .NET application and integrates with the full ASP.NET Core pipeline — dependency injection, authentication, rate limiting, OpenTelemetry, and custom middleware all apply. Routes and clusters are configured in appsettings.json or loaded dynamically from a database or service registry. Request and response transforms allow header manipulation, path rewriting, query modifications, and claim forwarding. YARP is an excellent fit for the Backend for Frontend pattern, internal API gateways in Modular Monolith decomposition, and migration facades in Legacy Modernisation.

concepts.title: Routes and clusters
concepts.description: A route matches an incoming request by path, host, or header and maps it to a cluster — a named group of destination backends with load balancing, health checks, and session affinity settings.

concepts.title: Transforms
concepts.description: Request and response transforms modify headers, paths, query strings, and the request body before forwarding or after receiving the upstream response — configurable in JSON or code.

concepts.title: Load balancing and health checks
concepts.description: YARP distributes traffic across cluster destinations using round-robin, least-requests, power-of-two, or random strategies and actively or passively monitors destination availability.

concepts.title: Dynamic configuration
concepts.description: Routes and clusters can be reloaded at runtime from any IProxyConfigProvider implementation — a database, Consul, or a custom control plane — without restarting the proxy process.

architecture.description: Inbound traffic hits the YARP middleware pipeline, which matches a route, applies transforms, forwards to the selected cluster destination, and returns the upstream response through the response transform chain.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: YARP is registered as middleware, routes are declared in configuration, and a custom transform forwards the authenticated user's claims to the upstream service as a trusted header.

bestPractices: Centralise cross-cutting concerns — authentication, rate limiting, correlation ID injection, and request logging — in the YARP middleware pipeline rather than duplicating them in every upstream service.
Use the dynamic configuration provider pattern to reload routes and clusters from a database or service registry at runtime, enabling zero-downtime topology changes without a proxy restart.
Apply path-strip transforms at the proxy rather than requiring upstream services to understand gateway-prefixed paths — each service should be independently addressable without the proxy prefix.
Monitor YARP's built-in metrics for request rate, error rate, and destination health alongside upstream service telemetry so the proxy itself is not a blind spot in the observability picture.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose YARP over Azure API Management?
interviewQuestions.answer: YARP is a good fit when the gateway logic is complex enough to need code, when deep ASP.NET Core middleware integration is required — custom auth, claim transforms, feature flags — or when a managed gateway's cost, latency, or networking constraints are not acceptable. APIM is better when a managed service, a developer portal, a built-in policy engine, and multi-region capabilities are needed without writing and operating gateway code.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Backend for Frontend pattern and how does YARP support it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Backend for Frontend creates a dedicated gateway per client type — web, mobile, third-party — each exposing the exact API shape that client needs, aggregating and transforming upstream responses. YARP supports this by letting each BFF be a .NET application with its own route configuration, transforms, and authentication policy, all sharing common middleware through the ASP.NET Core pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: How does YARP handle upstream service discovery in a dynamic environment?
interviewQuestions.answer: A custom IProxyConfigProvider implementation reads destination addresses from any source — a database, Consul, Kubernetes endpoints, or an Azure App Configuration store — and returns a new configuration on each poll. YARP watches for configuration changes and reloads routes and clusters without restarting, enabling dynamic registration and deregistration of upstream services.

note: YARP is a programmable proxy library, not a fully managed API gateway product — teams own its deployment, scaling, observability, and upgrades alongside the rest of the application.
tip: Use YARP as the strangler facade in a Legacy Modernisation — route new paths to modern services and old paths to the legacy system, then gradually shift routes as capabilities are migrated with no client-visible change.
warning: Placing authentication and authorisation exclusively in the YARP layer creates a single trust boundary — upstream services must still validate the forwarded identity header rather than treating an internal network call as implicitly trusted.
